docs.title: Thingstudio
docs.text:
Thingstudio is a visual, low-code way to program microcontrollers. You build a program, called a flow, in a node-based editor in your web browser. Nodes are functional blocks, and wires carry data between them. The design is inspired by Node-RED.

Thingstudio converts the flow to MicroPython, a version of Python for microcontrollers, compiles it and sends it to your board. The flow is saved on the board. It runs without the editor connected, and starts again after a reset or power cycle.

The editor: nodes to drag in on the left, your flow in the middle, and on the right the selected node's settings and the board's console. Click to see it full size. Tour the editor labels every part.

In practice, that means:

  • Local dev. Development happens locally; there is no cloud service.
  • Works offline. Once installed, it needs no internet connection, docs included.
  • Git friendly. Thingstudio's files, your programs and your board definitions, are plain, indented JSON that you save where you like. They diff cleanly and sit happily in a git repository. Passwords and other credentials are stored separately, so a committed program holds no secrets.
  • Made to be extended. Write your own custom nodes, and add your own boards and processors. You drop their files into a folder. There's nothing to rebuild.
  • Free and open source. Thingstudio is under the Apache 2.0 license. You can use it, change it and build on it, including in commercial products.

Already know the background?

If you know Node-RED, MicroPython or Arduino, read what's different for you, or go straight to Getting started.

  • Node-RED
  • MicroPython
  • Arduino and C

docs.title: What's different about programming with Thingstudio?
docs.text:
A typical microcontroller program, in Arduino for example, has a setup() section that runs once at boot, then a main loop that runs forever. The loop might:

  • read the sensors
  • check the buttons
  • update the outputs
  • check the network
  • go round again

Each new job makes the loop longer. A slow step, such as a network call, holds up everything else, and the timing gets hard to reason about.

Thingstudio programs respond to events instead. When a button is pressed, turn on a light. Every ten seconds, read the temperature. When a message arrives from the network, update the display. Each response runs only when its event happens, and the board waits for many events at once. This is event-driven programming.

MicroPython supports this style natively with asyncio. An asyncio program no longer reads top to bottom, which makes it harder to see what it does. Thingstudio's graphical editor of events, functions and outputs makes an event-driven program easier to build and follow.

docs.title: Events, nodes and wires
docs.text:
A program is made of nodes joined by wires. There are three types of node:

  • Sources start messages when something happens: a timer fires, a button is pressed, an MQTT message arrives.
  • Transforms take a message in and send a message on: a function, a filter, a delay.
  • Sinks act on a message: switch a pin, update a display, publish to MQTT.

A wire joins one node's output to the next node's input. The nodes and wires together make a flow. A flow can hold any number of chains, each starting at a source.

Nodes pass messages along the wires. A message is a dict, with its main value in payload. Messages are covered in more detail in flows, nodes and messages.

This way of working comes from Node-RED, a popular tool for home automation and IoT. In Node-RED, flows run on a server or a Raspberry Pi. In Thingstudio, they run on the microcontroller.

docs.title: Your own Python
docs.text:
The node reference lists the built-in nodes. For anything they don't cover, use a function node. It runs your Python on each message that arrives:

# payload arrives in degrees C, leaves in degrees F
msg['payload'] = msg['payload'] * 1.8 + 32
return msg

msg is a dict, with the main value in msg['payload']. Return it to pass it on, or return nothing to stop it. A function node can also keep state between messages and have more than one output.

To reuse code across flows, make it a custom node. A custom node has its own place in the palette and its own properties in the property panel. It can transform messages, act on them, or send them on a schedule.

You can also run Python directly on the board from the editor. See Commands and the Python prompt.

docs.title: Running on the board
docs.text:
The board runs MicroPython. You install it once, then Thingstudio adds a runtime of its own on top.

When you click Deploy, the editor turns your flow into MicroPython code and compiles it. It sends the result to the board over USB or WiFi, and the board swaps it in and starts running it. There's no firmware to flash, so changing a flow and trying it again takes seconds. The board keeps the flow and runs it again after a restart.

docs.title: Built on standard parts
docs.text:
Thingstudio tries not to reinvent the wheel.

  • MicroPython's asyncio provides the event-driven primitives.
  • Tried and tested libraries provide extra functionality and hardware drivers, such as Peter Hinch's mqtt_as and micropython-async, and drivers from micropython-lib.
  • What comes out is plain MicroPython. You can read it in the editor's Compiled source panel.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A board with an ESP32 or RP2040/RP2350 processor. Supported hardware lists what's been tested. Other boards that run MicroPython may work.
  • A USB cable that carries data, not only power.

docs.title: Writing flows with an AI assistant
docs.text: This page is for an AI assistant (or a person) writing a Thingstudio flow file or a custom node in the user's folder, without the editor. It is complete on its own, with two companions: the generated node catalog, and the thingstudio-compile command (Check a flow without the editor). With a board attached, device_cli.py deploys and runs the flow (Command line). The whole docs set is also one file at /llms-full.txt on the docs site, with an index at /llms.txt.

docs.title: Setting up your assistant
docs.text:
Paste this into the assistant's standing instructions (a project's instructions, AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, or a custom GPT/Gem), so it reads this page before it writes a flow:

When I ask for a Thingstudio flow or custom node, first read the Thingstudio authoring guide:
https://docs.thingstudio.net/ai-authoring/ (the whole docs set is one file at https://docs.thingstudio.net/llms-full.txt).
Write the flow as a .flow.json file, run the thingstudio-compile check with --board for my board and
--layout, fix every error and layout warning until it prints OK, then tell me: the board id you checked against, which credential
names I must create, what you assumed about wiring, and what you could not check.
Never say a flow works on the board unless you deployed it there and saw its output; otherwise say it
passes the check. No HTTPS in http_request.

Claude users can add the Thingstudio skill instead: thingstudio-flow-author-<version>.zip, from the releases page, carries this guide, the node catalog, the examples and the check command, so the assistant needs nothing else. Upload the zip as a skill in Claude, or unzip it into ~/.claude/skills/ for Claude Code. Use the skill whose version matches your editor. Otherwise the check needs Node and the built thingstudio-compile.mjs.

docs.title: The loop
docs.text:
1. Write the flow as a .flow.json file.
  2. Run node dist-cli/thingstudio-compile.mjs --board board:lolin-s2-mini --layout my.flow.json (the board ids are board:cyd, board:freenove-s3-4in, board:lolin-s2-mini, board:pico, board:pico-2 and board:pico-w, or processor:esp32, esp32-c3, esp32-s2, esp32-s3, rp2040, rp2350 for a bare chip; --list-boards shows the current list). Read every error: it names the node and says what is wrong. Fix them all, and every layout: warning, and run it again until it prints OK.
  3. Tell the user to open the file in the editor (File → Open), choose the board, and deploy. If a board is attached and the user asks you to test it, deploy it with device_cli.py instead, and report what the board printed. That result is for that board only.

The check is the same compile the editor runs, so a flow that passes it opens and compiles in the editor. It can't check credentials, custom node packages or the hardware. Don't claim a flow works on a board unless you deployed it there and saw it run; otherwise say it passes the check.

docs.title: The flow file
docs.text:
A JSON object. These keys matter:

Key What formatVersion 1 flowName A name for the flow. nodes [{ "id", "type", "properties" }]. id is any unique string. type is thingstudio/<kind>. edges [[fromId, outputNumber, toId, inputNumber]]. Numbers start at 0, in the order the catalog lists the ports. configs [{ "id", "type", "properties" }]: shared settings (I2C bus, WiFi, MQTT broker, touch panel). screens The pages of any GUI screen, keyed by that node's id. See GUI. panes, paneOf Optional. Tabs in the editor and which tab each node is on; leave them out and everything lands on one tab. When you edit a file that has them, put new nodes in paneOf too (copy the pattern). layout { "<nodeId>": { "pos": [x, y] } }. Optional, but give positions: without them every node lands at 0,0. notes Optional text shown in the editor's Notes panel. Say what the flow is for and how it is wired.

A property you leave out gets the default listed in the catalog. Use the catalog's names and types exactly: intervalMs, not interval. Values and ranges are checked by the compile, which says what is allowed.

Give every node a position, laid out as described in Layout.

A complete flow, a blinking LED on a LOLIN S2 Mini (its LED is pin 15):

{
  "formatVersion": 1,
  "flowName": "blink",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "tick", "type": "thingstudio/timer", "properties": { "intervalMs": 500 } },
    { "id": "flip", "type": "thingstudio/function",
      "properties": { "code": "msg['payload'] = msg['payload'] % 2\nreturn msg", "outputCount": 1 } },
    { "id": "led", "type": "thingstudio/gpio_out", "properties": { "pin": 15 } }
  ],
  "edges": [["tick", 0, "flip", 0], ["flip", 0, "led", 0]],
  "layout": { "tick": { "pos": [80, 200] }, "flip": { "pos": [300, 200] }, "led": { "pos": [520, 200] } },
  "configs": []
}

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
The user reads the flow on the editor's canvas, and the editor shows it exactly where the file puts it. It does not rearrange the nodes or zoom to fit. Lay it out the way a careful person would:

  • Left to right. Sources (timers, inputs, subscriptions) on the left, outputs on the right, and every wire running to a node further right. Don't wrap a long chain back to the left edge on a second row.
  • Columns about 220 px apart, left edge to left edge. Nodes are 84-132 px wide, so that leaves about 90 px for the wire. Use the same column positions for the whole flow, so columns line up.
  • Tight rows. Nodes are 34 px tall (a function node with several outputs is taller). Stack branches in one column about 36 px apart (y about 70 apart), and separate chains about 66 px apart (y about 100 apart).
  • One chain per job, stacked top to bottom: inputs and processing first, display or output last. Unwired nodes (GUI buttons that only appear on a screen, for example) go together at the bottom left.
  • Straight wires. A node fed by one node sits at that node's y. When one node feeds several, the first sits level with it and the rest stack below; a node fed by several sits level with the first of them, or between them.
  • Start near (80, 80), so the flow is on screen when it opens.

--layout checks these rules and reports problems as layout: warnings. --relayout rewrites the positions to follow them, which makes a good first pass for a new flow. When you edit the user's own flow, keep their layout: place only the nodes you add, and don't relayout it unless they ask.

docs.title: Which node
docs.text: To... Use send a message every so often, or once at start timer, startup, inject read a BME280 / BMP280 bme280 (payload is a dict with temperature, humidity, pressure; pick one out in a function) read another I2C chip i2c on a shared i2c-bus config react to a switch or button eswitch (a debounced switch: open and close events); ebutton for press, release, long-press and double-click; interrupt for raw edges drive a pin gpio_out (on/off), pwm_out change or route a message function; filter to pass only changes; delay keep a number's history journal, shown by a gui_trend show the time ntp (two for time and date: format time and date) talk MQTT / HTTP / UDP mqtt_publish, mqtt_subscribe, http_request, http_in and http_response, udp_send, udp_receive draw on a screen gui_screen with gui_* widgets, wired to display_spi

docs.title: Messages and the function node
docs.text:
Every message is a dict: msg = {'payload': ..., 'topic': ...}. payload is what nodes read; topic is a string, '' when there is nothing to say. Other keys ride along.

A function node's code is the body of a function in MicroPython (a subset of Python with a small standard library). Return msg to pass it on, or None to stop. With outputCount above 1, return a list with one entry per output (None for nothing, a list of messages for several). context keeps state for the node, flow for the whole flow. See function. A syntax error in the code is caught by the check.

A wire is refused if the payload types can't meet (for example a bool into a bytes input). The check reports it. Numbers go into bool inputs (zero is off), and an int into a number; a number into an int is refused.

Addresses are written two ways, because the nodes differ: the bme280 address is a plain number (118 is 0x76); a touch panel config's address is text ("0x38"). The catalog notes which.

A node that uses the network (mqtt_publish, http_request, http_in and so on) uses the flow's WiFi: add a WiFi config to configs and it is picked up; the node has no WiFi property of its own.

Things to know before you pick a node:

  • http_request is plain http:// only (no HTTPS), GET or POST. A reply with any status is passed on with an integer msg['status']; a failed connection or a timeout sends nothing on and logs an error. So test msg['status'] == 200 in a function, and expect no message at all when the server is unreachable.
  • mqtt_subscribe payloads arrive as text when they decode, otherwise bytes. For a number, use float(msg['payload']) in a function.
  • function code can import standard modules (json, framebuf, time) inside the body.
  • http_in gives a payload of None and http_response sets no Content-Type. Use port 80 unless something else on the board already uses it.
  • bme280 has no input: it reads on its own interval. To answer a web request with a current value, keep the latest reading with flow.set('temp', ...) in a function after the sensor, and read it with flow.get('temp') in a function between http_in and http_response (send a 503 before the first reading arrives).
  • To print text on a display_i2c (SSD1306), draw with framebuf in a function and send the buffer: see display i2c. Its address property is addr, a plain number (60 is 0x3C).

docs.title: Pins: take them from the board
docs.text:
Never guess a pin. List the boards with --list-boards, run --board-info board:<id> for what each pin does (the LED, the buttons, the display, the I2C pins) and which to avoid, and check the finished flow with --board board:<id>. If the user's board is not listed, say so, ask for the pins, and point them to the MicroPython documentation for their board (docs.micropython.org). Don't pretend a board is supported.

Things the pin check cannot catch: a pin that exists but is wired to something else on the user's board. When the user has told you the wiring, use it; when they haven't, say what you assumed.

docs.title: Config nodes and credentials
docs.text:
A node that needs shared settings names a config by id: "i2cConfigId": "cfg-i2c", with the config in configs:

{ "id": "cfg-i2c", "type": "thingstudio/config/i2c-bus", "properties": { "bus": 0, "scl": 15, "sda": 16, "freq": 100000 } }

The catalog lists each config type's fields. WiFi and MQTT configs hold a credential name:

{ "id": "cfg-wifi", "type": "thingstudio/config/wifi", "properties": { "credentialName": "home", "security": "password" } }

Never write a password, SSID or broker secret into a flow file. Write a credentialName and tell the user which names to create in the editor's credential store (they are saved there, not in the file). The check uses stand-ins for them and says so.

docs.title: GUI screens
docs.text:
A touch or plain display is two nodes wired together, gui_screen then display_spi, plus widget nodes (gui_label, gui_readout, gui_bar, gui_trend, gui_led, gui_button) that you wire data into. Where each widget sits is in screens:

"screens": { "<screenId>": { "pages": [
  { "name": "main", "root": { "kind": "column", "gap": 6, "padding": 4, "children": [
    { "kind": "text", "text": "Living room", "font": "font_body20" },
    { "kind": "widget", "node": "<readoutId>", "font": "font_digits48", "unitsFont": "font_body24", "alignSelf": "center" },
    { "kind": "spacer", "grow": 1 },
    { "kind": "pagedots", "alignSelf": "center" }
  ] } }
] } }

Rules that cause most failures:

  • The screen's width and height are the panel's own size (320 × 480 for the Freenove 4") whatever the orientation. Portrait needs nothing more: leave orientation empty and use the board's rotation (1 for the Freenove). To turn the picture, set the orientation property of display_spi to "90", "180" or "270" (clockwise), not the screen's size.
  • A navigate button's target is next, prev, back, home or the name of a page in screens; when you edit an existing flow, read the page names from its screens section.
  • Fonts: font_body12/16/20/24, font_digits16/24/32/48/64 (digits and a few symbols only), font_seg748/64/96 (seven-segment: 0-9 : . - and space). A character a font doesn't have is an error.
  • A widget is placed once per page, drawn the same on every page it is on. A label shows a value up to maxChars wide.
  • A page that doesn't fit gives an error that names the widget and page and how many pixels it needs. Use a smaller font or fewer things per row. Rows need the screen width minus the container's padding (in landscape on a 320-wide panel that is under 312 px).
  • With an orientation, xstart and ystart must be -1, which means "no offset" (the CYD example flow uses 0, which an orientation refuses; -1 is always allowed). At "90" or "270" the picture is the panel turned, so a 320 x 480 panel gives 480 wide by 320 high to lay out.
  • A modal is laid out in screens.<screenId>.modals, not in pages: see the format below.
  • A trend takes a journal's first output, and a journal takes numbers: sensor → journal → trend.

A modal (gui_modal, with screen set to the gui_screen node's id) is listed next to pages. Its root holds what it shows, and not the modal node itself:

"modals": [ { "node": "<modalNodeId>", "root": { "kind": "column", "padding": 8, "children": [
  { "kind": "text", "text": "Too hot", "font": "font_body24" },
  { "kind": "widget", "node": "<labelId>", "font": "font_body20", "maxChars": 20 }
] } } ]

Any message opens it; a message with payload None closes it; timeout (seconds, 0 for never) closes it by itself; a navigate button with target back acknowledges it. Its output sends 'ack', 'timeout' or 'closed'.

Placement keys, in screens:

Element Keys row, column children, gap, padding, align, justify, grow, alignSelf widget node (the widget node's id), font, unitsFont (readout), align and maxChars (label), height and minWidth (bar, trend), diameter (light), grow, alignSelf text text, font, align pagedots, spacer diameter, gap; width, height, grow

A button widget takes font, grow and alignSelf like the others. The button's own behaviour (mode, target, onValue, ...) is on the node: see the catalog. For a toggle that follows a real device (a smart plug), gui.md has the wiring.

Read GUI nodes for the details, and copy from test-flows/: gui-headliner-sensor-freenove-s3-4in.flow.json (a sensor display with trends, a clock and MQTT), gui-touch-freenove-s3-4in.flow.json (buttons), gui-orientation-test-freenove-s3-4in.flow.json.

docs.title: Custom nodes
docs.text: If no node does the job and a function node is not enough, write a custom node: <name>.node.json and <name>.node.py. Writing custom nodes is complete on its own. The two files go in ~/.thingstudio/custom-nodes/ on the computer running Thingstudio. The check command can't check them: read them against that page, and test the Python body on its own with sample messages.

docs.title: Examples to copy
docs.text: Task File in test-flows/ Blink an LED blink.flow.json Publish to MQTT basic-mqtt.flow.json Call a web service basic-http-request.flow.json A BME280 reading bmp280-test-flow.flow.json A sensor on a display, with trends and a clock gui-headliner-sensor-freenove-s3-4in.flow.json Touch buttons gui-touch-freenove-s3-4in.flow.json

docs.title: When you hand the flow back
docs.text: Tell the user, briefly: that it passes the check (and with which --board), which credential names to create, which board to choose in the editor, what you assumed about wiring, and what you could not check.

docs.title: Boards and processors
docs.text:
Each board and processor has a definition file that says which pins a flow may use. This page covers picking a board, seeing its pins, what gets checked, and writing your own definition files.

Thingstudio checks every pin in a flow against the board the flow is for. If a pin doesn't exist on that board, or using it would crash the board, the compile stops and says why.

Each board has a definition file, and so does each processor. Thingstudio comes with definitions for the boards and processors below. You can change them or add your own.

docs.title: Picking the board
docs.text:
Pick the board a flow is for from the Board menu in the toolbar. The default, Auto, uses the connected board. Auto recognises a board by the name MicroPython reports for it, and the menu shows what it found, for example Auto: LOLIN S2 Mini.

Some boards report only their processor. The CYD, for example, reports itself as a generic ESP32. Pick those boards from the menu by hand. You can also pick a processor without a board, for example ESP32 (any board).

The board menu picks pins, not memory. A classic ESP32 board with no PSRAM can run a GUI flow by flashing the custom firmware for classic ESP32, which carries the runtime and the flow libraries in the firmware.

A board picked by hand stays picked when you reconnect. If you then connect a board with a different processor, the menu goes back to Auto and the console says so.

If no board is connected and none is picked, pins are only checked against the range 0–48.

docs.title: Seeing a board's pins
docs.text:
Click Pins… next to the Board menu. It opens a page, in its own tab, for the board or processor picked there. The page lists, in order:

  • the pins the board names, such as its LED
  • for boards whose definition has a header, such as the Pico family, the physical pins, laid out like the board, with power and ground marked
  • every pin, with whether it's free, reserved or best avoided, and why
  • which pins each SPI and I2C bus can use

The page is read from the definition files each time you click. After changing a file, click Pins… again.

If Thingstudio knows the board's processor but not the board, the page shows the processor's pins and says the board's own ones, like its LED, are missing. It gives a starter file to add them: see Adding a board. If it doesn't know the processor either, the page says what the board reports: see Adding a processor.

docs.title: What gets checked
docs.text:
These stop the compile:

  • a pin the board or processor doesn't have
  • a reserved pin, such as a pin wired to the flash chip
  • an output on an input-only pin
  • an SPI or I2C bus the processor doesn't have, or a pin that bus can't use
  • an SPI speed the processor can't run on those pins

These give a warning, but the flow still compiles:

  • a pin to avoid, such as a strapping pin that changes how the board starts
  • a pull-up or pull-down on a pin that has no internal pull resistor

A node that needs hardware the board doesn't have, such as an ESP-NOW node on a Pico, is refused the same way. The palette greys out such a node while the board is known.

Warnings appear in the console when you deploy, and at the end of the compiled source.

In the properties panel, a pin field shows the board's name for that pin, such as LED. It also flags reserved pins and pins to avoid. On a board whose pins are named rather than numbered, the field is a dropdown of the board's pins. See Pins that aren't numbers.

docs.title: Built-in boards
docs.text: Board Processor Notes Raspberry Pi Pico RP2040 LED on GPIO 25 Raspberry Pi Pico W RP2040 GPIO 23, 24, 25 and 29 go to the WiFi chip. The LED isn't on a GPIO. Raspberry Pi Pico 2 RP2350 GPIO 0–29. LED on GPIO 25. LOLIN S2 Mini ESP32-S2 LED on GPIO 15, button on GPIO 0 LuatOS ESP32C3-CORE ESP32-C3 Pick by hand. LEDs on GPIO 12 and 13, button on GPIO 9. CYD (ESP32-2432S028, ST7789) ESP32 Pick by hand. Display, touch, SD, RGB LED and speaker pins are labelled. Freenove ESP32-S3 Display 4.0" (FNK0104S, ST7796) ESP32-S3 Pick by hand. Display and touch pins are labelled. 320x480, SPI bus 1. Rotation 1 is portrait. For landscape, set the display's orientation to 90 (or 270 for the other way up) and keep the screen and display at 320x480. Display and touch (FT6336U) work. Pyboard v1.0 STM32F405 Pins are named X1–X22 and Y1–Y12. The four onboard LEDs are on A13, A14, A15 and B4 (labelled LED_RED–LED_BLUE); the user switch SW is on X17. Seeed XIAO nRF52840 (Sense) nRF52840 Pins D0–D10 are labelled. RGB LED on 26, 30 and 6, on when the pin is 0. GPIO 20–25 go to the flash chip. Battery, IMU and microphone pins are labelled; IMU and microphone are on the Sense only. No WiFi. Wemos D1 R32 ESP32 Pick by hand. Pins carry their Arduino names, D0–D13 and A0–A5. A2–A5 are input only. LED on A0 (GPIO 2).

docs.title: Built-in processors
docs.text:
Processor GPIO Reserved ESP32 0–19, 21–23, 25–27, 32–39 (34–39 input only) 1, 3 (USB serial), 6–11 (flash) ESP32-S2 0–21, 26–46 (46 input only) 27–32 (flash) ESP32-S3 0–21, 26–48 27–32 (flash) ESP32-C3 0–21 12–17 (flash) RP2040 0–29 none RP2350 0–47 (0–29 on the RP2350A) none STM32F405 X1–X22, Y1–Y12 (named pins, not numbers) none nRF52840 0–47 (P1.x is 32 + x) none

The ESP32 runs SPI at up to 27 MHz on most pins. Faster speeds need the bus's own fast pins (SCK 14 and MOSI 13 on bus 1, SCK 18 and MOSI 23 on bus 2).

On the RP2040 and RP2350, each SPI and I2C bus can only use certain pins. The compile error lists the pins that work.

On the nRF52840, any pin works for SPI and I2C. SPI uses buses 2 and 3, up to 8 MHz; I2C uses buses 0 and 1.

The definition files list every pin to avoid, with the reason.

docs.title: Your definition files
docs.text:
Definition files live in ~/.thingstudio/boards/ and ~/.thingstudio/processors/. When Thingstudio starts, it copies in any built-in file that's missing, so you can read and edit them there.

To change a built-in board, edit its file. To get the original back, delete the file and restart Thingstudio. A newer version of Thingstudio doesn't update a file you already have, so delete a file to pick up its new built-in version.

Thingstudio reads these files when the editor starts, when you connect, and when you deploy. If a file has a mistake, it isn't loaded and the built-in is used instead. The console says what's wrong, and the Board menu lists the file under Invalid files.

docs.title: Adding a board
docs.text:
Save a JSON file in ~/.thingstudio/boards/. The file name, without .json, is the board's id. Use lowercase letters, digits, - and _.

{
  "name": "My weather station",
  "processor": "esp32-c3",
  "match": [],
  "pins": { "LED": 8, "SENSOR_SDA": 4, "SENSOR_SCL": 5 },
  "avoid": { "9": "Wired to the BOOT button." },
  "notes": "Hand-built, rev 2."
}

The fields are:

Field Meaning name Name shown in the Board menu. Required. processor Id of the processor, such as esp32 or rp2040. Required. match Board names MicroPython reports, for Auto. Use [] to pick the board by hand. Required. pins Names for pins, shown in the properties panel. Required, can be {}. capabilities Hardware this board adds to its processor, such as ["wifi"]. A board with no radio usually sets wifi to false instead. gpio The pins this board has, if fewer than its processor. For example ["0-29"]. reserved Pins that must not be used, each with a reason. avoid Pins that give a warning, each with a reason. free Pins the processor reserves or warns about that are fine on this board. For example ["12-13"] on an ESP32-C3 board whose flash doesn't use them. notes Anything else worth knowing. wifi false if the board has no WiFi. Hides connecting over WiFi for it. Leave it out if unsure. headerOrder "down" if the right-hand row is numbered top to bottom, like the left. Leave it out for a header numbered down the left and back up the right, like the Pico's. usb Where the USB connector is, with pin 1 at the top left: "top" or "bottom". Shown on the Pins… page. Needs header. header What each physical pin carries: a pin (a GPIO number, or a named pin), or a label such as "GND" or "3V3". Shown on the Pins… page. For example { "1": 0, "3": "GND", "40": "VBUS" }. A string that's one of the board's pins is that pin; any other string is a label.

Naming a pin in pins turns off the processor's warning for it, on the grounds that the board uses it on purpose. If the warning still matters, such as a strapping pin on a shield header, repeat it in the board's avoid.

Numbers in header are physical pin numbers, as printed on the board or its datasheet. A header numbered 1 to N is drawn in two columns, like the Pico's. For a board with several connectors, name the pins "P3-1" and so on.

Pin lists take numbers and ranges: [0, 2, "4-7"]. In reserved and avoid, the key is a pin or a range: { "6-11": "Wired to the flash chip." }. A processor whose pins are named uses the names in the same places: see Pins that aren't numbers.

To find the name MicroPython reports, connect the board and look for chipType in the console's [HELLO] line. The board name is the part before " with ".

docs.title: Adding a processor
docs.text:
Save a JSON file in ~/.thingstudio/processors/, named the same way as a board file. The built-in files in that folder are good examples.

The fields are:

Field Meaning name Name shown in the Board menu. Required. match Text in the processor name MicroPython reports, such as ESP32S3. Case, spaces and - are ignored. Required. nativeArch The mpy-cross -march value, such as xtensawin. Required. gpio Every pin the processor has. Numbers, or names on a processor whose pins aren't numbered. Required. inputOnly Pins that can't drive an output. noPull Pins without internal pull resistors. capabilities Hardware the chip has, such as ["wifi", "ble", "espnow"] or ["pio"]. A node that needs one the board lacks is refused. adc2 Pins on a second ADC that can't be used while WiFi is up (ESP32 family). reserved, avoid As for boards. spi, i2c Bus numbers, pins each bus can use, and SPI speed limits.

docs.title: Pins that aren't numbers
docs.text:
Some processors, such as the STM32 on a pyboard, name their pins (X1, A13) instead of numbering them. In a definition file, a pin is either a number, a range "4-7", or a name: a string that starts with a letter and contains only letters, digits, _ and -. Names go wherever numbers do — gpio, pins, reserved, avoid, a bus's pins — and a list can mix both. Ranges work for numbers only; list named pins one by one.

{
  "name": "Pyboard",
  "match": ["STM32F405"],
  "nativeArch": "armv7emsp",
  "gpio": ["X1", "X2", "X3", "X4", "Y1", "Y2", "Y3", "Y4"]
}

In the editor, a pin field on a named-pin board is a dropdown of the board's pins rather than a number input.

docs.title: Check a flow without the editor
docs.text: thingstudio-compile compiles and checks a flow file from the command line, with the same errors the editor gives. Use it in a script, in CI, or to let an AI assistant check a flow it has written.

docs.title: Build it
docs.text:
From the editor/ folder:

npm ci
npm run build:cli

This writes dist-cli/thingstudio-compile.mjs, one script that needs only Node 22 or later.

docs.title: Use it
docs.text:
node dist-cli/thingstudio-compile.mjs my-flow.flow.json

A good flow prints one line:

OK  my-flow.flow.json: 25 nodes, 21 wires, 4 configs, 38980 bytes of MicroPython, 0 warnings

A bad one lists every problem it found:

FAIL  my-flow.flow.json: 2 errors
  error: wire from node t1 output 4 to node g1 input 1: node t1 has no output 4 (it has 1)
  error: node x1: unknown node type "thingstudio/teleporter"

The exit code is 0 for a valid flow, 1 for a flow with errors, and 2 for a bad command or a file it can't read.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
• --board board:freenove-s3-4in checks pins against that board. --list-boards shows the choices. Without a board, pins are checked against the widest range and a warning says so.
  • --board-info board:freenove-s3-4in prints that board's labelled pins (the LED, the display, the I2C pins), the GPIOs that exist, and the ones to avoid or that are reserved, as JSON.
  • --out flow.py writes the generated MicroPython.
  • --json prints the result as JSON: ok, errors, warnings, notes, stats and the source.
  • --strict makes warnings fail the check.
  • --layout also checks the layout: wires run left to right, nodes are close but don't overlap, and the flow starts on screen. Problems come back as layout: warnings (so --strict fails on them). The rules are in Layout.
  • --relayout rewrites each file's node positions to follow those rules, then checks it. It changes positions only, and it overwrites the file.
  • --describe timer prints a node's type, ports and properties with their defaults. --describe-all prints every node and config node (add --json for JSON). The same list is on the node catalog page, generated from the code.
  • --no-syntax skips the MicroPython syntax check. --arch sets its -march (default xtensawin).

docs.title: What it checks
docs.text:
• The file is a flow file, and every node type exists.
  • Every wire joins real ports, and is one the editor would accept. The editor drops a wire it refuses when it opens the file.
  • A property the file leaves out gets the editor's default, as when you open the file in the editor.
  • The flow compiles: pins, properties, GUI layouts, nodes with nothing wired to them.
  • The generated code is valid MicroPython. This uses the same mpy-cross the editor deploys with, and catches a typo in a function node's code before you deploy.

docs.title: What it doesn't check
docs.text:
• WiFi and MQTT credentials. The secrets are in the backend, so the check uses stand-in values and says so in a note. A missing credential shows up when you open the flow in the editor.
  • Custom node packages. A flow that uses one fails with "unknown node type".
  • A real board. It can't tell you the display is wired right, or that the memory is enough. Deploy does that; Command line can deploy and run a flow without the editor.

docs.title: Command line
docs.text: Options for starting Thingstudio, a way to install the runtime and run flows without the editor, and a check for a flow file. To check a flow file from the command line, see Check a flow without the editor.

docs.title: Starting options
docs.text:
Add these after thingstudio (or thingstudio-backend, from source). thingstudio --help lists them all.

Option What it does --no-browser Don't open the editor in a browser. Open http://127.0.0.1:8765/ yourself. --port N Serve the editor on port N instead of 8765. --data-dir DIR Use DIR instead of ~/.thingstudio. See The Thingstudio folder. --log-level LEVEL How much Thingstudio prints in its terminal: DEBUG, INFO (default), WARNING or ERROR.

If you restart Thingstudio with the editor still open, that tab reconnects and no new one opens.

docs.title: Installing the runtime from the command line
docs.text:
Useful for scripting, or setting up several boards at once. It needs a copy of the source repository. Click Disconnect in the editor first, so the port is free.

pip install mpremote
python3 test-flows/deploy_runtime.py --port PORT

PORT is the board's port, as shown in the editor's port list. When it finishes, click Connect in the editor.

device_cli.py runtime install does the same thing and resets the board afterwards; see below.

docs.title: Deploy and run a flow without the editor
docs.text:
device_cli.py is a small command line for a board on USB serial. It does what the editor does, without a browser: find the board, check the runtime, deploy a flow, fire inject nodes, run console commands and watch the output.

python3 test-flows/device_cli.py list          # USB serial ports
python3 test-flows/device_cli.py hello         # runtime version, chip, running flow
python3 test-flows/device_cli.py flow deploy my-flow.flow.json \
    --mpy-cross ~/mpy-src/mpy-cross/build/mpy-cross
python3 test-flows/device_cli.py trigger inject0001
python3 test-flows/device_cli.py exec "settings.namespaces()"
python3 test-flows/device_cli.py watch
  • If there is one USB serial port, --port is not needed. Use --port or THINGSTUDIO_PORT otherwise.
  • flow deploy compiles the .flow.json with the same compiler as the editor, then deploys it. It takes the flow name from the file's own flowName. That name is also the settings namespace, so check it is what you expect.
  • --trigger NODE_ID (repeatable) fires inject or startup nodes after deploy, for testing without clicking.
  • --json prints one JSON object per line, for scripts.
  • Disconnect in the editor first: only one program can hold the serial port.
  • flow deploy needs a native mpy-cross. The build recipe is in device-runtime/test/README.md, or set THINGSTUDIO_MPY_CROSS to one you already have.

python3 test-flows/device_cli.py <command> --help lists every option. test-flows/README.md has ready-made test flows and their expected output.

docs.title: Step 4: Connect your board
docs.text:
Connect the board over USB so the editor can talk to it. Start Thingstudio if it isn't running: see step 1.

To connect:

  1. Plug the board in.
  2. Check the port list in the toolbar. When the editor opens it looks for boards, and selects yours if it's the only USB device plugged in. If you plugged the board in afterwards, click ⟳ next to the port list.
  3. Click Connect. It changes to Connected · Disconnect. Click that to disconnect.

With more than one USB device plugged in, pick your board from the port list. Port names depend on your operating system and the board's USB chip. To tell which port is your board, unplug it, click ⟳, plug it back in and click ⟳ again. The port that appears is your board.

docs.title: What the console says
docs.text:
A board with MicroPython but no Thingstudio runtime gives this message:

No reply from the runtime. MicroPython but no Thingstudio runtime: Tools → Install runtime…

You install the runtime in the next step.

If the console says nothing came back, or the board replied but isn't running MicroPython, go back to step 3: install MicroPython. Other messages are explained in Board won't connect.

Once the runtime is installed, the console shows which flow the board is running, if any.

Once a board with WiFi is set up, you can also connect to it over WiFi. See Connecting over WiFi.
