docs.title: Custom firmware for classic ESP32
docs.text:
A MicroPython image with Thingstudio's runtime and every flow library built in, for classic ESP32 boards with no PSRAM. It is what lets those boards run a GUI flow: stock MicroPython runs out of memory loading the display stack.

The image is optional. Stock MicroPython and the runtime install work as usual, and nothing in the editor changes. Use it when a flow on a 4 MB ESP32 stops with MemoryError and the steps in MemoryError or a library that won't load have not helped — this is the third of them, "run a firmware image with the libraries built in".

The technique is not specific to this image or to this chip: freezing the runtime and the flow libraries into MicroPython works on any board. This image exists because a classic ESP32 is the board where it changes the most, and because building one needs an ESP-IDF toolchain. firmware/classic-esp32/ in the repository is a working example to copy for another board.

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
The runtime and the flow libraries are frozen into the firmware, which means MicroPython runs them from flash instead of copying them into RAM. On a classic ESP32 that is the difference between a GUI flow starting and failing with MemoryError allocating 13317 bytes.

Because the libraries are already there, Deploy does not send them. The console says so after connecting:

[libraries] this flow uses font_body12, … st7796py -- already on the board: font_body12, … st7796py

Two things follow from that, and both matter on a board with this little RAM:

  • Deploying over a running GUI flow works. On stock MicroPython it fails: the runtime and the flow fight over the same memory.
  • The first deploy after flashing has more memory to work with than any later one, because the board is not drawing yet. Judge a flow by a deploy over another flow, not by the first one.

The image carries no board-specific settings. Pins and the display come from the board definition, so one image serves any classic ESP32 board. It is tested on the CYD.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
You need these:

  • A classic ESP32 board with 4 MB of flash and no PSRAM (ESP32-D0WD and similar). This image is not for the S2, S3, C3 or C6, and not for RP2040 or RP2350 boards.
  • A USB cable that carries data.
  • esptool and mpremote on the computer: pip install esptool mpremote.
  • Four downloads from the project's releases page: the image, its .sha256 file, _deps.json and main.py.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
Flashing erases the board: its saved flows, board settings and WiFi credentials are gone afterwards.

  1. Download the four files from the releases page: the image, its .sha256, _deps.json and main.py. Put them in one folder and go there. Check the image against its checksum:
IMAGE=thingstudio-classic-esp32-13.1.0-dad343f.bin
shasum -a 256 -c "$IMAGE.sha256"      # sha256sum -c on Linux
  1. Put the board in download mode if your board needs it, then write the image at address 0:
esptool.py --chip esp32 --port /dev/ttyUSB0 write_flash 0x0 "$IMAGE"

On macOS the port looks like /dev/cu.usbserial-14420. On Windows it is COM3 or similar.

  1. Write the files that live on the filesystem, not in the image:
mpremote connect /dev/ttyUSB0 fs cp main.py :/main.py
mpremote connect /dev/ttyUSB0 fs mkdir :/lib
mpremote connect /dev/ttyUSB0 fs cp _deps.json :/lib/_deps.json

main.py is the boot script: it starts the runtime that is frozen into the firmware. A board with the image and no main.py starts at the Python prompt instead.

_deps.json is the list of libraries the board has, so Deploy skips them. Without it Deploy sends its own copies, which works but uses the memory the image was meant to save.

  1. Reset the board. It starts the listener and prints LISTENER_READY.

The repository also has firmware/classic-esp32/install.sh, which runs these steps in one command. Read it before running it: it erases the filesystem partition, and its port name comes from PORT.

docs.title: Connect and deploy
docs.text:
Connect in the editor as usual. Two things confirm the image is running:

  • the console's version line reports runtime 12.1.0 or later
  • [libraries] … already on the board: … names every library the flow imports

Then deploy the flow. A GUI flow that failed with MemoryError on stock MicroPython should run.

docs.title: Memory and the board
docs.text:
The image does not add RAM. A classic ESP32 has about 140 KB free for flows with this image and nothing running, and a GUI flow takes most of what it has. Measured on the CYD (ESP32-D0WD, 4 MB, no PSRAM), in KB:

Board state MicroPython free Largest block ESP-IDF free ESP-IDF largest Just booted, no flow 142 105 129 108 GUI flow running 108 50 70 52 GUI flow running, after two more deploys 120 27 18 14

Read the third row before leaning on deploys: each deploy over a running flow leaves the heaps more fragmented, and the chip's own heap shrinks as MicroPython takes from it. A GUI flow still starts (a 9.5 KB flow needs far less than the 27 KB block), but WiFi draws from that shrinking chip heap, and the console warns when it is low.

Two habits avoid the limits that remain:

  • Keep frames small. The gui screen node sends a frame in strips for exactly this reason; a function node that builds a whole frame as one buffer still needs that buffer to be contiguous.
  • When a deploy fails with MemoryError, the console says how much memory the board had. If the board cannot make room, remove the flow and power cycle before deploying again. A soft restart does not help: it reuses the same heap. A power cycle also returns the chip heap that repeated deploys take.

docs.title: Back to stock MicroPython
docs.text: Flash a standard MicroPython build for the board, then install the runtime again. The stock flow of Installing MicroPython to Install the runtime covers both steps. Flashing erases the board's flows and settings, as above.

docs.title: Reporting a problem
docs.text: Reports on any classic ESP32 board are welcome, listed or not. Include the board's name and the console's version and [memory] lines from a fresh boot.

docs.title: Writing a custom node for Thingstudio
docs.text: A custom node is two files sharing a base name: <name>.node.json (the descriptor) and <name>.node.py (the behavior), placed in the backend's ~/.thingstudio/custom-nodes/ directory. Thingstudio loads it for you, and you drag it onto the canvas like any built-in node.

docs.title: Loading a custom node
docs.text:
Put both files in ~/.thingstudio/custom-nodes/ on the computer running Thingstudio.

The editor loads every package in that folder when it starts, and again when you switch back to its window. After changing a file, you can also click Reload custom nodes at the bottom of the palette. The console lists what loaded. Each node appears in the palette under its group.

A package with a problem isn't loaded, and the console says which file and why. The others still load. If two packages use the same type, the first one by file name is loaded and the other is reported.

The folder starts with two examples, doubler and dht22, under examples in the palette. Read them, change them or delete them. Thingstudio adds them only the first time it runs, so deleted examples stay deleted.

docs.title: The descriptor: <name>.node.json
docs.text:
Example — a node that doubles a numeric payload:

{
  "type": "custom/doubler",
  "kind": "transform",
  "label": "doubler",
  "color": "#6e3b8a",
  "bgcolor": "#3f1f4a",
  "icon": "×2",
  "ports": {
    "inputs": [{ "name": "msg", "type": "any" }],
    "outputs": [{ "name": "msg", "type": "any" }]
  },
  "properties": [
    { "name": "factor", "label": "factor", "kind": "number", "default": 2 }
  ]
}

type (required) — unique id, shaped namespace/name (lowercase letters, digits, underscores). Must not start with thingstudio/ — reserved for built-in nodes.

kind (required) — one of:

  • source — generates messages on its own. 0 input ports, 1 output port. Must declare a numeric intervalMs property (below) — unless eventSource is true (it waits on an event) or runOnce is true (it runs once at flow start).
  • transform — one message in, one or more out. 1 input port, 1+ output ports.
  • sink — consumes a message, produces nothing. 1 input port, 0 output ports.

label (required) — name shown on the canvas and in the palette.

title (optional) — the canvas title, when it should differ from label.

hidden (optional) — hide the node from the palette (a flow file can still use it).

description (optional) — a short line shown at the top of the property panel, like a built-in node's own description.

presetType / screenOutline (optional) — show a save/load-preset control or the screen-layout outline in the property panel, as the relevant built-in nodes do.

color / bgcolor (optional) — CSS colors for the node's outline and fill. Default is gray.

icon (optional) — one or two characters shown in the icon chip.

group (optional) — which palette section the node sorts into. Defaults to "general". Any name works; a new one gets its own section, added after the built-in ones.

priority (optional) — a number controlling order within group, lower first. Omit it and the node sorts after every built-in node in that group.

ports.inputs / ports.outputs — arrays of { name, type }. type is one of int, number, bool, string, bytes, any — the same types built-in nodes use, with the same wire-compatibility checks. Use any when unsure.

A port type can follow a select property instead of being fixed:

{ "name": "msg", "type": { "property": "payloadType", "map": { "bool": "bool", "number": "number" }, "default": "bool" } }

The value of property picks the wire type; an unset or unmapped value uses default. The property must be a select field, and every key in map must be one of its options.

A transform may declare more than one output. Return a list to route messages across them, Node-RED style (e.g. return [msg, None] sends to output 1 only). A source has one output; a sink none.

properties (optional) — fields shown in the property panel when the node is selected:

{ "name": "factor", "label": "factor", "kind": "number", "default": 2 }
  • name — identifier. Your Python reads the value by this key.
  • label — shown in the property panel.
  • kind — text, textarea, number, boolean, select, configRef, pin, or target.
  • default — used when a node instance doesn't set the property. Type must match kind.
  • options — required for select: array of { value, label }. default must be one of the values.
  • configType — required for configRef: the config type the picker offers (e.g. thingstudio/config/i2c-bus). At compile time the picked config's own properties become a dict the node reads — see below.
  • singleton — optional, on a configRef: resolve the flow's one config of configType at compile time instead of an id you store (how a built-in uses the shared WiFi setting). Zero or two such configs is a compile error.
  • pinUse / pinPull — optional, on a pin: input or output, and the pull (none/up/down). Adding pinUse makes the compiler claim the pin, so two nodes can't quietly set the same pin up two ways. A pin without pinUse is just a value (checked to exist on the board) — use that for a bus line like SCL/SDA.
  • target — a kind for a board-specific node. Its value in Python is a dict of the board/processor this flow is compiled for — boardId, boardName, processorId, processorName, label, capabilities — or None if no board is chosen, so guard for that. Use it to identify your exact board (e.g. a XIAO nRF52840's own IMU).
  • nodeId — a kind whose Python value is this node's own id (a string). Use it to report status about yourself: runtime.report_status(properties['id'], 'connected').
  • help / placeholder / min / max / step / optional / rows — optional, the same panel hints a built-in field has. rows sets a textarea's height (default 4). pin fields take a number default; optional marks one where -1/blank means "not wired".
  • visibleWhen — optional: show the field only when another property satisfies a condition, e.g. { "field": "mode", "equals": "deadband" }. Operators: equals, notEquals, in (an array), gt, gte, lt, lte.

A polled source node must declare a numeric property named intervalMs — it sets the poll interval. An eventSource or runOnce source does not need one.

docs.title: The behavior: <name>.node.py
docs.text:
Ordinary MicroPython. Define exactly one top-level function, named for your node's kind:

  • transform / sink → async def run(msg, properties):
  • source → async def emit(properties):

msg is a dict with a payload key, a topic key, and room for any extra keys you add. topic is a routing/identification string — the mqtt subscribe built-in node, for instance, fills it with the real MQTT topic a message arrived on. Most nodes have no natural topic of their own; set it to '' rather than a real value. The key is required either way — don't leave it out. properties is a dict of the node instance's configured values.

Transform — return the (possibly modified) msg, or None to stop it propagating:

async def run(msg, properties):
    msg['payload'] = msg['payload'] * properties['factor']
    return msg

Sink — return value is ignored:

async def run(msg, properties):
    print('got:', msg['payload'])

Source — called once per intervalMs, must return a msg:

async def emit(properties):
    return {'payload': 42, 'topic': ''}

Anything else — imports, helper functions, setup code — is ordinary Python.

docs.title: Example: a temperature sensor source
docs.text:
temp_sensor.node.json:

{
  "type": "myproject/temp_sensor",
  "kind": "source",
  "label": "temp sensor",
  "ports": { "outputs": [{ "name": "msg", "type": "number" }] },
  "properties": [
    { "name": "pin", "label": "data pin", "kind": "number", "default": 4 },
    { "name": "intervalMs", "label": "read interval (ms)", "kind": "number", "default": 5000 }
  ]
}

temp_sensor.node.py:

import dht
import machine

_pin = properties['pin']
_sensor = dht.DHT22(runtime.shared('pin', _pin, ('dht22',), lambda: machine.Pin(_pin)))

async def emit(properties):
    _sensor.measure()
    msg = {'payload': _sensor.temperature(), 'topic': ''}
    msg['humidity'] = _sensor.humidity()
    return msg

The sensor is built once, at setup, not on every emit() call — top-level code and emit share the same properties.

Temperature goes in payload, not humidity, because payload is the field the port's declared type (number, here) checks against, and the field a generic downstream node reads — debug prints msg['payload'] and nothing else, whatever else is in msg. Put whichever value you want wired and type-checked that way in payload. Anything else is a passenger: humidity rides along in the same msg, but only a node written to look for it specifically will ever read it.

docs.title: nonlocal, not global
docs.text:
Your file's top-level code doesn't run at true module scope — each node instance gets its own wrapper function, so two instances of the same custom type never share state. To keep a value across calls, use nonlocal:

_count = 0

async def emit(properties):
    nonlocal _count
    _count += 1
    return {'payload': _count, 'topic': ''}

global raises NameError here — there's no module-level name to find.

docs.title: Pins and buses
docs.text:
Get a pin or bus with runtime.shared(kind, key, settings, make), not by building it yourself. The first node to ask builds it with make(); every later node gets the same object. If a later node asks with different settings, the flow stops with an error naming both, instead of one node quietly changing the pin under another.

_pin = runtime.shared('pin', 5, ('in', 'up'), lambda: machine.Pin(5, machine.Pin.IN, machine.Pin.PULL_UP))
_i2c = runtime.shared('i2c', 0)  # fetch a bus another node in the flow set up

The built-in nodes use these settings: ('in', 'none' | 'up' | 'down') and ('out', 'none') for pins, and () for an ADC (runtime.shared('adc', 26, (), lambda: machine.ADC(machine.Pin(26)))). Pins, ADC, PWM, I2C and SPI all work this way: see Hardware is shared.

docs.title: Sharing a config (I2C bus, touch panel)
docs.text:
A configRef property lets your node pick one of the flow's config nodes. Its value in properties is that config's own properties as a dict (or None if none is picked), so a custom I2C node can join the same bus a built-in i2c/bme280 node uses:

{ "name": "bus", "label": "I2C bus", "kind": "configRef", "configType": "thingstudio/config/i2c-bus", "default": "" }

_i2c = runtime.shared('i2c', properties['bus']['bus'])  # the flow's shared bus, by its number

The bus/pins come from the config; keep the same runtime.shared key a built-in would use so a clash is reported, not silently shared. (Network configs — WiFi, MQTT — expose only the credential's name, not the secret, so a custom node can't make a WiFi connection from one.)

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
If your node opens something that needs closing on redeploy — a socket, typically — register it:

import socket

_sock = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
runtime.register_cleanup('my_node_socket', lambda: _sock.close())

async def run(msg, properties):
    _sock.sendto(str(msg['payload']).encode(), ('192.168.1.50', 9000))

runtime is already available — no import needed. Without cleanup, a redeployed flow can leave the old socket open and fail with EADDRINUSE on the next deploy.

docs.title: Persisting values
docs.text:
runtime.settings keeps a value across reboots and redeploys of the same flow. Use it for an application setting a user changes on the device — units, a colour scheme — not for per-message state, which belongs in a closure local.

async def run(msg, properties):
    units = runtime.settings.get('units', 'kg')   # the default is yours, not the store's
    runtime.settings.set('units', msg['payload'])
    msg['payload'] = units
    return msg

Values are namespaced by the deployed flow's name, so a different flow cannot read or overwrite them. Renaming the flow starts a fresh namespace. A missing key returns your default. set raises SettingsError if the board cannot save (full or read-only flash) — let it surface as a node error rather than assuming the write worked. delete(key) and keys() round out the surface.

The store is a plain key/value; it does not know what a value means. Save only what the user changed, and supply the default at the read. To clear stored values, see debugging.

docs.title: Event-driven sources
docs.text:
A source that reacts to something other than the clock sets "eventSource": true and defines a second function, async def wait(properties), alongside emit. wait is awaited, so it blocks until your event fires; then emit builds the message. No intervalMs is needed.

{
  "type": "custom/button",
  "kind": "source",
  "label": "button",
  "eventSource": true,
  "ports": { "outputs": [{ "name": "msg", "type": "bool" }] },
  "properties": [{ "name": "pin", "label": "pin", "kind": "pin", "default": 11, "pinUse": "input" }]
}

A hardware interrupt (machine.Pin.irq) is the usual reason to use eventSource. Bridge it into asyncio with the vendored ThreadSafeEvent — its set() is the one call safe in a hard-IRQ handler — and register the handler:

import machine
from threadsafe_event import ThreadSafeEvent   # pushed with the flow because you import it

_evt = ThreadSafeEvent()

def _irq(_pin):
    _evt.set()          # a hard-IRQ handler may only do this: no allocation, no print, nothing else

_pin = runtime.shared('pin', properties['pin'], ('in', 'up'),
                      lambda: machine.Pin(properties['pin'], machine.Pin.IN, machine.Pin.PULL_UP))
_pin.irq(trigger=machine.Pin.IRQ_RISING, handler=_irq)

async def wait(properties):
    await _evt.wait()
    _evt.clear()

async def emit(properties):
    return {'payload': True, 'topic': ''}

runtime.asyncio.Event() is fine when the event is set from other asyncio code; for a real IRQ use ThreadSafeEvent, which survives the hard-IRQ context.

Keep any state the two share at the top of the file (both functions come from one per-instance closure, so nonlocal works across them).

docs.title: Run-once sources
docs.text:
A source that runs once, at flow start, sets "runOnce": true instead. It defines only emit; Thingstudio calls it once, with no intervalMs and no wait.

{
  "type": "custom/boot",
  "kind": "source",
  "label": "boot",
  "runOnce": true,
  "ports": { "outputs": [{ "name": "msg", "type": "string" }] }
}

docs.title: Two-faced nodes
docs.text:
A sink with "eventSource": true both consumes and produces: one input, one output, and three functions in .node.py. run(msg, properties) handles the input; wait(properties) then emit(properties) produce the output. All three come from the same per-instance closure, so they share state through nonlocal.

{
  "type": "custom/gateway",
  "kind": "sink",
  "label": "gateway",
  "eventSource": true,
  "ports": {
    "inputs": [{ "name": "msg", "type": "any" }],
    "outputs": [{ "name": "msg", "type": "string" }]
  }
}

Use it when the node has to react to messages and also act on its own (a clock that echoes a message and then ticks, or a subscription you can change at run time). A transform cannot be two-faced.

docs.title: Compile time: <name>.compile.py
docs.text:
A package can also include an optional compile-time hook, <name>.compile.py, defining one function:

def compile(ctx, properties):
    return {"properties": {...}, "errors": [...]}

It runs in the editor when the flow is compiled — never on the board. properties is what the flow file holds for this node; ctx describes the flow:

  • ctx["node"] — this instance: id, type, properties, and wired (a boolean per input/output).
  • ctx["flow"]["nodes"] / ["configs"] — every node and config, with non-secret properties only.
  • ctx["nodesOfType"] — every node of this node's type in the flow, including this one: id, type, and non-secret properties. Use it when the nodes share a decision (for example, a port's set of routes).
  • ctx["referencedConfigs"] — the full properties (including credentials) of the configs this node's configRef fields point at.
  • ctx["target"] — the board/processor being compiled for, or None.

Return a dict (or None). Everything is optional:

Key Meaning properties Extra values merged into what .node.py receives. Keys your descriptor doesn't declare are allowed. claims [{"resource": "GPIO 22", "use": "my device"}], checked like a pin field. warnings Strings shown in the compile warnings. errors Strings that stop the compile, naming the node.

The hook is sandboxed: no files, network, clock or randomness. Its result is data only — it cannot return Python or change the generated code's shape. Limits: 64 KB of properties, 64 claims, 32 warnings and 32 errors, and one second per hook; a hook that runs too long is stopped.

wifi status is an example: its hook derives the flow's WiFi config and whether an MQTT node is present, so its Python never asks you for the network twice.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
Load time — a malformed .node.json is rejected immediately, with a message naming what's wrong: bad type, wrong port count, missing intervalMs, and so on.

Compile time — a bad property value on a specific node instance (e.g. a non-numeric number field) errors out naming that node and property.

Deploy time — .node.py is spliced into the flow as-is; Thingstudio doesn't check it. A typo surfaces as a runtime error (e.g. NameError) reported from the device, attributed to your node.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
A polled source node's emit runs on a fixed intervalMs schedule; an eventSource source waits on wait instead.

Two instances of the same custom node get independent setup. For a pin field that declares pinUse, Thingstudio checks it against the board and claims it at compile time; a pin you build in Python yourself (or read from a plain number field) it can't see, so use runtime.shared() for those, and a clash is caught when the flow starts.

Custom node Python runs with the same trust as any other node, including Thingstudio's function node. Loading a package only adds it to the palette; its Python runs on a board only when you place the node and deploy. Only files you place in the folder are loaded — there's no registry and no URL install — so don't put a package there that you haven't read.

docs.title: Debugging & troubleshooting
docs.text: What the console and compiled source show, and what to do when a board or deploy fails.

docs.title: Console and compiled source
docs.text:
The console shows what the board and Thingstudio report: deploy results, node errors, and what debug nodes and print() send. Clear empties it.

Its Show menu sets how much it shows:

  • Normal: your flow's output, warnings, errors, and the results of what you do, such as a deploy.
  • Info: adds routine reports: board detected, versions, memory, libraries sent, network status.
  • Debug: adds raw protocol messages and the board's boot output.

Hidden lines are kept, so choosing Info or Debug later shows what was already logged.

The Compiled source panel shows the MicroPython your flow compiles to.

The editor's version is next to its name in the toolbar, and in Help → About Thingstudio. A + after it means you built it from uncommitted changes. Include the versions when you report a problem.

docs.title: Memory
docs.text: With Show set to Info, a [memory] line after each connect and deploy shows the board's free RAM. On an ESP32 it also shows the ESP-IDF heap and its largest free block. WiFi, MQTT and TLS use the ESP-IDF heap, not MicroPython's. If WiFi won't join while MicroPython has plenty free, a low ESP-IDF figure is the likely cause. The FAQ explains where an ESP32's memory goes.

docs.title: Commands and the Python prompt
docs.text:
The command box under the console runs Python on the board. Type a line and press Enter; the result appears in the console. The up and down arrows bring back earlier commands.

gc.mem_free()
import machine; machine.Pin(15).value()
os.listdir()

Commands run alongside your flow, and variables you set stay for the next command. A command that takes time, such as a sleep or a loop, holds up the flow until it finishes.

The stored application values are available as settings:

settings.namespaces()      # each flow's name and how many values it holds
settings.clear()           # clear the current flow's values
settings.clear_all()       # clear every flow's values

Use these if a saved value is wrong, or a flow you no longer deploy left values behind. Clearing takes effect immediately; the next read returns the default. Tools → Clear device settings… does the same from the editor: choose the current flow, or every flow.

For MicroPython's own >>> prompt, click Stop flow & open prompt. The flow and the runtime stop; nothing is deleted. What you type in the box now goes to that prompt, and Deploy is off. Click Restart Thingstudio to start the runtime and the saved flow again.

To use the prompt from another program, such as Thonny or mpremote, click Connected · Disconnect first.

docs.title: Watching a board start up
docs.text:
To see a board's own startup messages, connect with mpremote connect PORT and no further command, or a serial monitor that doesn't send Ctrl-C when it opens. A working runtime prints LISTENER_BOOTING, then LISTENER_READY.

mpremote repl and Thonny's Shell interrupt the board as they connect, which looks like a board that never starts. Close them before connecting from Thingstudio: only one program can use the port at a time.

docs.title: Board won't connect
docs.text:
When Connect, Tools → Check status or Tools → Install runtime… gets no proper reply, the console says what the board sent instead, and what to do:

Console says What to do Nothing came back Usually no MicroPython. Install MicroPython. If it's there, press reset, then Tools → Check status. MicroPython but no Thingstudio runtime Tools → Install runtime…. MicroPython replied but didn't enter install mode Press reset and install again. Board is in its bootloader An ESP32 in download mode. Press reset, not BOOT. If it repeats, install MicroPython. Board runs CircuitPython, or replied but not as MicroPython Install MicroPython. Runtime still starting Wait, then Tools → Check status. Install stalled Replug the board, click ⟳, and try again. If it repeats, restart Thingstudio.

If the port itself won't open, the console says why:

Console says What to do port in use Close other serial monitors, IDEs, or editor tabs using the board. port access refused Replug the board and check port permissions. On Linux, check you're in the dialout group. board gone from that port Check the cable, click ⟳, and connect again.

The raw error stays in the message, in brackets. Include it if you report a problem.

docs.title: Deploy is grayed out
docs.text:
Compile → Deploy is grayed out when:

  • the editor isn't connected to a board;
  • the flow on the board is the one on the canvas, deployed and unchanged since;
  • the flow is stopped at the Python prompt (click Restart Thingstudio);
  • the board is restarting.

docs.title: Module missing on the board
docs.text:
A deploy can fail with ImportError: no module named '...': the flow needs a module the board's MicroPython doesn't have. The board keeps running its previous flow.

The usual cause is networking. MQTT, UDP, HTTP and WiFi nodes need the network and socket modules, which only boards with WiFi or Ethernet have. A Raspberry Pi Pico has neither; a Pico W does. If the board reports no WiFi, the console warns you before the deploy.

Other modules differ between ports and builds. If the import is in your own function node, check the module exists for your board in the MicroPython docs. A board that should have it may need a different MicroPython build.

Thingstudio's own libraries, such as the MQTT client and display drivers, are sent by Deploy. See Libraries.

docs.title: MemoryError or a library that won't load
docs.text:
A board can be short of memory while its [memory] line still shows free RAM. The free RAM is in pieces, and a flow or a library needs one piece big enough to fit. This is common on boards with little RAM, most of all on an ESP32 without PSRAM once a display flow has run.

When a deploy fails this way, work through these in order:

  1. Tools → Remove flow… — so nothing is resumed at start-up.
  2. Power cycle the board — unplug its USB cable and plug it back in, or Tools → Reset board (hard).
  3. Deploy again.

Removing the flow alone does not help: the running flow keeps its memory until the chip restarts. A soft restart does not help either — it restarts the interpreter over the same heap regions and gives no chip memory back. Only a power cycle gives the board a clean heap, which is why it is the step above.

If it still fails after the power cycle, the flow may be too big for this board. That is a limit of the board, not a fault in the flow. Three things can still work:

  • Make the flow smaller. Fewer pages in the GUI, fewer libraries imported, a smaller frame. The gui screen node sends a frame in strips for this reason; a function node that builds a whole frame at once still needs one big block.
  • Use a board with more memory. Boards with PSRAM have room for flows a board without it cannot start.
  • Run a firmware image with the libraries built in. On a classic ESP32 there is a ready-made one: Custom firmware for classic ESP32. On other boards the same technique works — freeze the runtime and the flow libraries into MicroPython — if you build your own.

If none of those is possible, the flow does not fit that board. Nothing in the editor can make room that the board does not have.

Deploy does not try to fix this for you: it reports the failure and stops, because freeing or restarting on your behalf would leave the board in a state you didn't choose. When the board looks short of memory before a deploy starts, the console says so in one line (only 19 KB free on the board, this flow is 10 KB -- it may not fit) and deploys anyway. That figure is total free memory, not the largest free block, so it is a hint rather than a verdict.

docs.title: WiFi Internal State Error on deploy
docs.text: On an ESP32, deploying a flow with MQTT nodes can fail with "Wifi Internal State Error". The board is still reconnecting to the network the previous flow used, and refuses a new connection until that finishes. The MQTT nodes retry up to three times. If it still fails, deploy again.

docs.title: Deploy resends a piece, or fails part-way
docs.text:
Deploy sends the flow, and each library it uses, in pieces, and waits for the board to confirm each one. Over a USB-serial chip such as the CYD's, a piece can arrive damaged or its confirmation can get lost. The console then shows resending (1/2), and Deploy carries on. That is normal now and then.

If a piece still fails after three tries, Deploy stops and says so, and the flow on the board is unchanged. Deploy again. If it keeps happening, try another USB cable or port, close anything else using the serial port, or connect over WiFi.

docs.title: The console shows [protocol] illegal or PROTOCOL_ILLEGAL
docs.text: The editor and the board follow a fixed set of moves when they talk. A line starting [protocol] illegal (from the editor) or PROTOCOL_ILLEGAL (from the board) means one of them made a move that isn't in that set. It is a bug in Thingstudio, not something you did. Deploy carries on or fails cleanly either way. Please report it with the console lines around it.

docs.title: Reading a node error
docs.text: When a node fails on the board, the console shows a [NODE_ERROR] line naming the node and the error, and the node is highlighted on the canvas. Network nodes (udp send, udp receive, http request, mqtt publish, mqtt subscribe) also name the operation and the host and port. A network node error without them is worth reporting.

docs.title: I2C device not answering
docs.text:
A sensor node's status dot shows disconnected, with "no reply at 0x76", when nothing answers at its address. Scan the bus to see what is there. Type these two lines in the command box, one at a time, with your bus and pins:

i2c = machine.I2C(0, scl=machine.Pin(5), sda=machine.Pin(4))
[hex(a) for a in i2c.scan()]

An i2c device node set to scan does the same from a flow.

An empty list means nothing answered. Check these, in order:

  • The pin numbers. On a Pico, GP4 and GP5 are physical pins 6 and 7.
  • SDA and SCL swapped.
  • Power (3.3 V) and ground to the device.
  • Solder joints on the header pins.

An address different from the node's means the address is wrong, not the wiring.

docs.title: A toggle button goes back
docs.text:
A gui toggle with its input wired shows the state you asked for until the input confirms it. If nothing arrives within wait for confirmation (5 s by default), it goes back to its last state, shows a cross for a moment, and the console shows NODE_ERROR ... NoConfirmation: no confirmation within 5 s.

Check these, in order:

  • The device is reachable and the command reached it. Watch the command topic with a debug node.
  • The input is wired to the device's state topic, not the command topic.
  • The state is sent in a form the toggle matches. A toggle set to true and false ignores ON and OFF: set its value type to text.

docs.title: Native code (Tools → Native code)
docs.text:
The gs4, gs2 and mono frame formats of display spi compile part of their code to native machine code, which needs the right architecture for the board's chip.

Tools → Native code defaults to Arch: Auto, which uses the processor of the board in the Board menu. If Deploy fails with an architecture or native-module error, pick your board's chip from the list and deploy again.

docs.title: Restarting the board
docs.text:
A board can run short of memory after several deploys, or after a flow that uses a lot of it, such as a display. The console suggests a restart when a deploy fails with MemoryError, the board restarts while starting a flow, or an ESP32 has too little memory left for WiFi.

The Tools menu has two restarts:

  • Tools → Restart board (soft) restarts MicroPython. The saved flow starts again with a clean interpreter: the flow's own objects are gone, but the heap regions are the same ones and memory MicroPython took from the chip is not returned. USB stays connected.
  • Tools → Reset board (hard) resets the whole chip, like its reset button, and frees all memory. A board with native USB (Pico, ESP32-S2, S3 and C3) disconnects; click Connect when it's back.

A soft restart is enough to clear a flow's own leftovers, such as a big buffer a faulty node left behind. It is not enough for a board that cannot fit a deploy: nothing short of a full power cycle gives the memory back in one piece, so that case is Remove flow…, power cycle, deploy (above). When an ESP32 is short of memory for WiFi, only the hard reset helps either. The console says which to use. Deploy is off until the board is back, which can take several seconds.

docs.title: Board stuck restarting
docs.text:
A flow that crashes the board as it starts would crash it on every restart. If the saved flow doesn't stay up for 10 seconds on three restarts in a row, the board starts without it, and the console shows [safe mode]. Fix the flow and deploy it again, or remove it.

Tools → Remove flow… deletes the saved flow from the board, for any flow that stops the board answering:

  1. Select the board's port and choose Tools → Remove flow….
  2. If the console asks, press the board's reset button. Thingstudio keeps trying for a minute.
  3. When it's done, click Connect.

The board then starts with the runtime only, as after a fresh install. The flow on your canvas isn't affected.

docs.title: Step 2: Tour the editor
docs.text:
A tour of the editor, naming each part of the screen. Start Thingstudio if it isn't running: see step 1.

The parts of the editor. Click to see it full size.

docs.title: Toolbar
docs.text:
The toolbar runs left to right in the order you work: the flow, the board, then deploy.

  • New, open, save: the File menu.
  • This flow's name: saved with the flow. The board reports it, so you can tell which flow it's running.
  • Connect to a board: pick the board's port from the list, then click Connect. ⟳ looks for boards again.
  • Board type, pin map: the Board menu sets the board the flow is for; Auto uses the connected board. Pins… opens a page listing that board's pins.
  • Deploy flow to board: Compile → Deploy turns the flow into MicroPython and sends it to the board.
  • Board tools, user guide: the Tools menu has board jobs, such as installing the runtime or removing a flow. The Help menu opens this user guide.

docs.title: Palette
docs.text:
Nodes to add: every node, in groups such as General, Network and Hardware. Drag a node onto the canvas, or click it. Type in the filter box to find one. Custom nodes appear in the group they name, or in General.

Click a group's name to fold or open it. Only General starts open. The editor remembers which groups you opened, in this browser. While you type in the filter box, every group with a match opens.

docs.title: Canvas
docs.text:
The canvas is where you build the flow. The tabs above it, Sheets of this flow, spread one flow across several sheets.

The canvas works like this:

  • Wire two nodes: drag from one node's output, on its right, to another node's input, on its left.
  • Select: click a node or a wire. Ctrl-click to select several nodes.
  • Delete: select, then press Delete or Backspace. Deleting a node removes its wires too.

The editor refuses a wire between ports whose types don't fit. See Wiring.

docs.title: Properties, notes and console
docs.text:
The right-hand side holds the selected node's settings and what the board sends back:

  • Selected node's settings: the properties panel.
  • Notes on this flow: the Notes panel, free text saved with the flow.
  • Generated MicroPython: the Compiled source panel. Click it to open it.
  • Messages from the board: the Device console, with messages from Thingstudio and the board, including your flow's output. Its Show menu sets how much it shows: Normal for your flow's output, results and errors, Info to add routine reports such as memory, Debug for everything.
  • Run Python on the board: type a line of Python and click Send. It runs on the board alongside the flow. See Commands and the Python prompt.
  • Escape to REPL: Stop flow & open prompt stops the flow and gives you MicroPython's own >>> prompt. Restart Thingstudio starts the flow again.

To make the notes, compiled source and console column wider or narrower, drag its left edge. Double-click the edge to reset it.

Editor in depth covers wire types, node labels, presets, config nodes and node status.

docs.text: Step 3: install MicroPython on your board.

docs.title: Why does my ESP32 have so little free memory?
docs.text:
An ESP32's RAM is shared between MicroPython and the chip's own software: ESP-IDF, its FreeRTOS scheduler, and the WiFi stack. About half of a classic ESP32's 520 KB is taken before anything runs, by code that has to run from RAM, the flash cache and fixed buffers. WiFi and the rest of ESP-IDF then take more as they run.

Measured on a CYD (classic ESP32, no external RAM) with a flow running:

KB Used before the heap starts ~287 MicroPython's heap 109 ESP-IDF, FreeRTOS and WiFi, allocated while running ~85 Free 33

So MicroPython gets about a fifth of the chip's RAM. The [memory] line in the console (shown at the Info level) shows the current figures.

docs.title: Why does a Pico W have more room than an ESP32-C3, when the C3 has more RAM?
docs.text: The Pico W's WiFi chip has its own processor and memory. On an ESP32 the whole WiFi stack runs on the main chip and uses its RAM. So a 264 KB Pico W leaves more for your flow than a 400 KB ESP32-C3.

docs.title: Deploy failed with "MemoryError ... allocating 38400 bytes". Why, when there's more free memory than that?
docs.text: Free memory is in pieces. A big buffer needs one piece that size, and after a while an ESP32 may not have one. A 240x320 frame in 16 grays is 38,400 bytes. The GUI nodes avoid this by drawing the screen in strips. If your own function node builds a full frame, draw it in strips too, or restart the board before deploying.

docs.title: Why doesn't Deploy clear the old flow or retry when the board runs out of memory?
docs.text: Because a repair nobody asked for hides the limit. The editor used to stop the running flow and retry when a deploy didn't fit; the retry then failed a step later, and the board was left stopped without anyone deciding that. Now a deploy that doesn't fit fails once, with the board's free-memory figure, and the console says what to do. The steps are yours to take: Tools → Remove flow…, power cycle the board (unplug and replug the USB cable, or Tools → Reset board (hard)), then deploy. See MemoryError or a library that won't load.

docs.title: Why isn't a soft restart enough after "too full to receive the flow"?
docs.text: Because a soft restart reuses the same heap. It restarts the interpreter, so the flow's own objects go away, but the heap regions MicroPython took as it grew stay where they were, and memory taken from the chip is not given back. A board that couldn't find one big block before the soft restart still can't after it. Only cutting power to the chip rebuilds the heap from scratch — hence the power cycle in the recipe above.

docs.title: Deploy failed a second time. Is the flow too big for my board?
docs.text:
Possibly, yes. Work through this in order:

  1. Tools → Remove flow…, then power cycle the board (unplug and replug the USB cable, or Tools → Reset board (hard)), then deploy.
  2. If it still fails, the flow may be too big for the board. Make it smaller (fewer GUI pages, fewer libraries, a smaller frame), use a board with more memory, or — on a classic ESP32 — run the custom firmware, which keeps the runtime and the libraries in the firmware.

Boards with little RAM have a point where a flow simply does not fit. Nothing in the editor can make room the board does not have. The console shows how much memory the board had when it failed; see MemoryError or a library that won't load.

docs.title: Why is Deploy sending the flow in pieces?
docs.text: Some boards (classic ESP32 with no PSRAM) can't take a whole flow in one message once a display flow has run: the memory is free but in pieces too small for one message. Deploy sends the flow in 5 KB pieces instead, each confirmed before the next. Larger pieces keep a deploy quick; a board that can't take 5 KB has a memory problem worth seeing rather than one to work around.

docs.title: Why does http request fail with "MemoryError" fetching a page?
docs.text: The node reads the whole response body into memory at once. A page larger than the largest free block fails, even when the console shows more free memory than the page size. A 56 KB page on an ESP32-C3 failed with MemoryError allocating 56722 bytes; a 48-byte page worked. Point the node at a smaller response, or use a board with PSRAM for large pages.

docs.title: My ESP32-S3 board has PSRAM, but the console shows only about 120 KB free. Why?
docs.text: The firmware doesn't use the PSRAM. The generic ESP32-S3 build leaves it off. Flash the build for boards with octal PSRAM (the SPIRAM_OCT variant) from micropython.org/download. The console then shows megabytes free. Freenove's S3 display boards are an example: 121 KB before, 7.8 MB after.

docs.title: Which board should I use for a display and WiFi together?
docs.text: An ESP32 with external RAM (PSRAM), such as many ESP32-S3 boards. MicroPython puts its heap in the external RAM, leaving the chip's own RAM for WiFi. A classic ESP32 or ESP32-C3 without PSRAM can run a display and WiFi, but only at lower color depths and with little to spare.

docs.title: My WiFi flow worked before, but now the board crashes or won't join. Why?
docs.text: On an ESP32, MicroPython's heap grows by taking memory from ESP-IDF when a flow needs more, and keeps it until the chip is reset. After a flow that uses a lot of memory, such as a display, WiFi may not have enough left to start. The console warns you before you deploy. Use Tools → Reset board (hard): a soft restart doesn't give that memory back. See Restarting the board.

docs.title: Why does opening a flow ask "Save changes to …?" even though I changed nothing?
docs.text: That is the browser's file-permission dialog, not the editor. A page may read a file you pick, but to write it back (Save) it needs your permission, and the browser asks with that wording: "Save changes to gui-hero-cyd.flow.json? https://127.0.0.1:8765 will be able to edit it." Accept it to let the editor save back to that file. It is not about unsaved changes on the canvas, and it comes back after a page refresh because browsers grant file access per page session. Opening from Open… or Recent is the same file; nothing is written until you press Save.

docs.title: Why does Deploy say the board needs the runtime installed again?
docs.text: The editor and the runtime on the board talk a shared protocol. When an update changes it, a board with the older runtime can't run flows from the newer editor, so Deploy stops and says so. Use Tools → Install runtime…, then Connect and deploy again.

docs.title: How do I tell which version of the editor I'm running?
docs.text: It's next to Thingstudio in the toolbar, and in Help → About. A + after it means you built the editor from uncommitted changes.

docs.title: My clock shows -- and never the time. Why?
docs.text: The ntp node hasn't synced yet. Its status says why: waiting for WiFi, or NTP from server failed when the board can't reach the server. It tries again every 30 seconds. See ntp.

docs.title: My gui toggle shows --. Why?
docs.text: A toggle with its input wired shows -- until the input sends a value it recognises. It matches the input against its on sends and off sends values, true and false unless you changed them. A Tasmota plug reports ON and OFF as text: set the toggle's value type to text. See a toggle that follows the real device.

docs.title: Why can't I use a touch node and a gui screen on the same panel?
docs.text: Both would poll the same chip, and each would take touches from the other. A gui screen reads its panel itself. Use the touch node only when you aren't using the GUI. Deploy stops and names both nodes if a panel is picked twice.

docs.title: Why won't a function node's output wire into pwm out?
docs.text: A function node's output has the type any, and pwm out's input takes a number. The editor refuses a wire from any to number, int or string inputs. See Wiring.

docs.title: Why is Compile → Deploy grayed out after a deploy?
docs.text: The board already runs the flow on the canvas. Deploy comes back when you change the flow. See Deploy is grayed out.

docs.title: Why are the pin fields dropdowns?
docs.text: Your processor names its pins instead of numbering them. The STM32 on a pyboard uses X1, A13 and so on. Pin fields then list the chip's own pins rather than take a number. See Pins that aren't numbers.

docs.title: Why can't I use SPI bus 0 or 1 on an nRF52840?
docs.text: On the nRF52840, SPI 0 and 1 share hardware with I2C 0 and 1, so a flow using both would fail on the board. Thingstudio offers SPI on buses 2 and 3 only. See Boards and processors.

docs.title: Why did my saved settings reset after I renamed the flow?
docs.text: Saved values are kept per flow name. Renaming the flow makes it a new name to the board, so its values start from the defaults. The old values are still on the board: rename the flow back to use them again, or clear them from the command box.

docs.title: Why doesn't my Uno TFT shield work on a Wemos D1 R32?
docs.text: The D1 R32 puts the shield's A2, A3 and A4 on GPIO 35, 34 and 36, which are input only on an ESP32. A parallel TFT shield drives its RS, CS and RST lines from those pins, so it can't start. Wire GPIO 15 to A2 (RS), GPIO 33 to A3 (CS) and GPIO 32 to A4 (RST), then set those pins in the display node.

docs.title: Step 6: Blink an LED
docs.text:
Your first flow: make an LED blink once a second, using three nodes.

Your board should be connected, with the runtime installed: steps 4 and 5.

docs.title: Find your LED's pin
docs.text:
Many boards have an LED wired to a GPIO pin. To find it, click Pins… next to the Board menu. Pins that the board names, such as LED, are listed first. Supported hardware lists the boards Thingstudio has definitions for. For any other board, check its documentation.

The Pico W and Pico 2 W LEDs are wired through the WiFi chip, not a GPIO pin, so gpio out can't reach them. On those boards, or any board without an LED, wire an LED and a 330 Ω resistor from a free GPIO pin to GND. The LED's longer leg goes towards the GPIO pin.

Don't leave out the resistor. Without it, the LED draws too much current and can damage the board.

docs.title: Build the flow
docs.text:
1. Drag a timer onto the canvas. Set interval (ms) to 500.

  2. Drag a function onto the canvas. Replace its code with:

    msg['payload'] = msg['payload'] % 2
return msg

  3. Drag a gpio out onto the canvas. Set pin to your LED's GPIO number.

  4. Wire timer → function → gpio out.

docs.title: Deploy
docs.text:
Click Compile → Deploy. A successful deploy ends like this in the console:

[deploying "my flow" as 3f2a…]
[deploy OK -- flow is running on the device]

The flow name and ID will differ. Set the console's Show menu to Info or Debug to see each stage, including the board's free memory.

The LED now blinks: on for half a second, off for half a second.

The flow keeps running on the board after you unplug it from your computer and power it another way.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
The timer sends a message every 500 ms. Its payload is a count: 1, 2, 3, and so on.

gpio out turns the pin on for any payload that isn't zero. Wired straight to the timer, the LED would switch on and stay on.

The function node turns the count into 1, 0, 1, 0 with % 2. That gives on, off, on, off.

docs.title: Try these changes
docs.text:
Each change below edits the flow you built. Deploy after each one.

  • Change the timing. Set the timer's interval (ms) to 100, or 2000 for a slower blink.

  • Read the pin instead of counting. Replace the function's code with this, using your LED's GPIO number in place of 2. Each message sets the LED to the opposite of what the pin reads now.

    import machine
msg['payload'] = 0 if machine.Pin(2).value() else 1
return msg

  • Keep your own state. Replace the function's code with this. context stores a value between messages, private to this function node. See Context, flow and settings.

    on = not context.get('on', False)
context.set('on', on)
msg['payload'] = on
return msg

The function node keeps nothing from one message to the next. In the first version the state is the timer's count, in the second it's the pin, in the third it's context. A flow keeps state only where you put it: in a message, on the hardware, or in context.

docs.title: If it doesn't blink
docs.text:
Each symptom below has its own fix:

  • Deploy is grayed out: you aren't connected, so click Connect. Deploy is also grayed out after a deploy until you change the flow, while the flow is stopped at the Python prompt (Stop flow & open prompt), and while the board restarts.
  • Compile fails: usually a mistake in the function node's code, such as a missing quote or wrong indentation. The console shows the Python error in red, with its line, and highlights the node. Fix the code and deploy again.
  • Deploy works, then the console shows [NODE_ERROR]: the code ran on the board and failed, for example on a misspelt name. The message names the error, and the node is highlighted.
  • Deploy fails: the console says why. See Board won't connect.
  • Deploy works but the LED stays dark: check the pin number against Pins…. Some boards' LEDs light when the pin is off; the LED still blinks, the other way round.

For anything else, see Debugging & troubleshooting.

docs.title: Flow lifecycle
docs.text: How a flow is saved, opened, deployed and disconnected.

docs.title: Save and open
docs.text:
A flow is saved in a .flow.json file you choose, so it can live in a project's git repo like any other file. The file holds the nodes and their properties, the wiring, the canvas layout and the config nodes.

  • File → Save (⌘S, or Ctrl+S on Windows and Linux) writes to the flow's file. A new flow has no file yet, so the first Save asks where, like Save As. The file's name shows next to the flow name.
  • File → Save As… (⇧⌘S, or Ctrl+Shift+S) always asks where, and that file becomes the flow's file.
  • File → Open… (⌘O, or Ctrl+O) loads a flow file. Save then writes back to it.
  • Open recent, in the File menu, lists the last 8 files you opened or saved, newest first, with each one's flow name. After a reload the browser asks once for permission to use the file again. A file that has moved or been deleted is taken off the list. Clear recent files forgets the list, not the files.
  • File → New flow starts an empty flow with no file.

If the file has changed on disk since you opened or last saved it, for example after a git checkout, Save asks before overwriting it. Say no and use Save As to keep both.

The recent list is kept in your browser, so another browser or a private window has its own. Safari and Firefox can't save back to a file: there, Save and Save As download the flow, Open uploads one, and there's no recent list.

The flow name field is saved inside the file itself and is sent with every deploy, so a connected board's identity is visible in the console instead of a bare deployment id. It also suggests a filename for Save As (spaces and punctuation become dashes), but you can type over that suggestion freely.

Custom node packages and saved credentials live in ~/.thingstudio/custom-nodes/ and ~/.thingstudio/credentials/. They're shared across flows rather than tied to one project, unlike a flow itself — a saved credential referenced by name from a config node is never written into the .flow.json file. See The Thingstudio folder.

docs.title: Deploy
docs.text:
Compile → Deploy compiles the current canvas to MicroPython bytecode and sends it to the connected board, replacing whatever flow is currently running there.

A successful deploy shows a confirmation in the console and the new flow starts running immediately. A failed deploy leaves the board's current flow running and shows a specific error:

  • a compile error — something in the flow itself, such as a missing required property
  • a space error — the compiled flow doesn't fit in the board's available flash/RAM
  • a library error — see below

After a successful deploy the button grays out: the board is already running exactly what's on the canvas. It re-enables the moment you change anything (a property, a node, a wire). A failed deploy leaves it enabled so you can fix the problem and retry.

docs.title: Libraries
docs.text:
Some nodes need a library on the board, such as MQTT or a display driver. Deploy installs the libraries your flow uses and removes ones it no longer uses, so a board holds only what its flow needs. The console lists them on each deploy. A library already on the board isn't sent again.

A function node that imports one of these libraries, such as import mqtt_as, gets it the same way. If the board can't take a library, for example because its flash is full, the console names the library and says why.

Tools → Check status re-requests the board's identity — chip type, runtime version, and whichever flow is currently running — without resetting the board or redeploying anything. Useful for confirming what's actually on the board after reconnecting to a session already in progress.

Disconnect closes the serial connection. The board keeps running whatever flow was last deployed; disconnecting the editor doesn't stop it.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
From a new board to a blinking LED, in six steps:

  1. Install Thingstudio on your computer.
  2. Tour the editor: what each part of the screen does.
  3. Install MicroPython on your board.
  4. Connect your board to Thingstudio.
  5. Install the runtime, the part of Thingstudio that runs on the board.
  6. Blink an LED: build your first flow and deploy it.

You need a board that runs MicroPython, and a USB cable that carries data, not only power. Supported hardware lists the boards Thingstudio is tested on.

docs.title: Step 1: Install Thingstudio
docs.text:
Thingstudio is a program you run on your computer. It opens its editor in your web browser. It brings its own Python, so nothing else needs installing to run it.

There are two ways to install it. Both give you the same program.

  • Download a package and unpack it. Nothing runs until you start it.
  • Run the installer script. It picks the right package, checks its checksum, and adds a thingstudio command. Run it again to upgrade.

docs.title: Download a package
docs.text:
Download the package for your computer from the releases page. Installation details lists the package for each platform.

macOS and Linux: unpack it with tar -xzf thingstudio-VERSION-PLATFORM.tar.gz. Thingstudio is the thingstudio file in the unpacked folder.

Windows: unzip it anywhere, for example into your Documents folder. Thingstudio is thingstudio.cmd in the unzipped folder. If Windows says "Windows protected your PC", click More info, then Run anyway. The Windows package isn't signed.

docs.title: Run the installer script
docs.text:
The commands below download the installer script and pipe it straight into a shell. To read the script before running it, download install.sh or install.ps1 and open it in a text editor.

macOS and Linux: run this in a terminal. On a Mac, that's the Terminal app, in Applications → Utilities.

curl -fsSL https://github.com/mkarliner/ThingStudio/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh

If the installer says ~/.local/bin isn't on your PATH, run the command it prints, then open a new terminal.

On Linux, your account must be in the dialout group (uucp on Arch) to use USB boards. The installer reports this if your account isn't in the group, and prints the command to fix it.

Windows: open PowerShell from the Start menu and run this. It doesn't need administrator rights.

irm https://github.com/mkarliner/ThingStudio/releases/latest/download/install.ps1 | iex

To upgrade or remove Thingstudio, or build it from source, see Installation details.

docs.title: Start Thingstudio
docs.text:
How you start Thingstudio depends on how you installed it:

  • Installer script: run thingstudio in a terminal. If the command isn't found, open a new terminal and try again.
  • Package on macOS or Linux: run ./thingstudio in the unpacked folder.
  • Package on Windows: run thingstudio.cmd in the unzipped folder.

The editor opens in your browser at http://127.0.0.1:8765/. Leave the terminal open while you work. Press Ctrl-C there to stop Thingstudio.

Thingstudio also serves this user guide, so it works offline. Help → User guide opens it.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Step 2: tour the editor.

docs.title: Installation details
docs.text: How Thingstudio is packaged, where it puts its files, how to upgrade and remove it, and how to build it from source. Getting started has the install steps.

docs.title: Packages
docs.text:
Each release has a package for each platform:

Platform Package macOS, Apple Silicon (M1 and later) thingstudio-VERSION-macos-arm64.tar.gz macOS, Intel thingstudio-VERSION-macos-x86_64.tar.gz Linux, x86_64 thingstudio-VERSION-linux-x86_64.tar.gz Linux, ARM 64-bit (Raspberry Pi 4 and 5 on a 64-bit OS) thingstudio-VERSION-linux-aarch64.tar.gz Windows, x86_64 thingstudio-VERSION-windows-x86_64.zip

SHA256SUMS lists each package's checksum. The macOS packages are signed and notarized by Apple.

A package doesn't add a thingstudio command; start it from its folder, or by its full path. To upgrade, replace the folder with a newer one. To remove it, delete the folder. On Linux, add your account to the dialout group (uucp on Arch) yourself to use USB boards.

docs.title: Installer script
docs.text:
On macOS and Linux, the installer puts Thingstudio in ~/.local/share/thingstudio and the thingstudio command in ~/.local/bin. Your settings live in ~/.thingstudio (see The Thingstudio folder).

On Windows, it puts Thingstudio in %LOCALAPPDATA%\Thingstudio and adds the thingstudio command to your PATH. Your settings live in %USERPROFILE%\.thingstudio.

To upgrade, run the installer script again.

To remove Thingstudio on macOS and Linux:

curl -fsSL https://github.com/mkarliner/ThingStudio/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh -s -- --uninstall

On Windows:

& ([scriptblock]::Create((irm https://github.com/mkarliner/ThingStudio/releases/latest/download/install.ps1))) -Uninstall

Upgrading and removing never touch ~/.thingstudio, or your flows, which are saved wherever you chose.

docs.title: From source
docs.text:
For working on Thingstudio itself. You need Python 3.10 or later, Node.js 22.12 or later, and make. On a Mac, make comes with the Xcode command line tools (xcode-select --install).

In the repository folder, run make. This builds the editor and the user guide, installs Thingstudio into a .venv folder, and puts the thingstudio-backend command on your PATH. Run make again after updating the repository. It only rebuilds what changed. If your python3 is older than 3.10, name a newer one: make PYTHON=python3.12.

Start it with thingstudio-backend, or make run. On a Mac, start it from Apple's Terminal app. macOS blocks WiFi connections from a copy run from source in other terminals, such as iTerm.

docs.title: Step 3: Install MicroPython
docs.text:
Thingstudio runs on top of MicroPython, so the board needs it first. You install it once per board.

A new board usually doesn't have MicroPython. If yours already has it, or you're not sure, go to step 4. If MicroPython is missing, the console says so when you connect, and links back here.

docs.title: Get the firmware
docs.text:
Download the firmware for your board from micropython.org/download. Pick your exact board if it's listed, or the generic build for your chip:

Chip Generic build File type ESP32 ESP32_GENERIC .bin ESP32-S2 ESP32_GENERIC_S2 .bin ESP32-S3 ESP32_GENERIC_S3 .bin ESP32-C3 ESP32_GENERIC_C3 .bin RP2040 (Pico, Pico W) RPI_PICO, RPI_PICO_W .uf2 RP2350 (Pico 2, Pico 2 W) RPI_PICO2, RPI_PICO2_W .uf2

For any other chip, see Other microcontrollers.

docs.title: RP2040 and RP2350: drag and drop
docs.text:
Copy the firmware onto the board as a file:

  1. Hold the BOOTSEL button while you plug the board into USB.
  2. A drive called RPI-RP2 (or RP2350) appears.
  3. Copy the .uf2 file onto it.

The board restarts into MicroPython by itself.

docs.title: ESP32 family: esptool
docs.text:
If Thingstudio is connected to the board, click Disconnect first. Only one program can use the board's port at a time. If another program has it open, esptool reports Resource busy or could not open port.

Install esptool once:

pip install esptool

Erase the flash, then write the firmware. ADDRESS depends on the chip:

esptool.py --port PORT erase_flash
esptool.py --port PORT --baud 460800 write_flash ADDRESS firmware.bin
Chip ADDRESS ESP32, ESP32-S2 0x1000 ESP32-S3, ESP32-C3 0

PORT is the board's serial port. On macOS and Linux it starts with /dev/, on Windows it's COM followed by a number. To find it, run esptool.py flash_id with no --port: esptool searches for the board and prints the port it found.

If esptool can't talk to the board, put it into download mode and try again: hold BOOT, press and release RESET, then release BOOT. Boards with a separate USB-serial chip usually do this by themselves. If writing fails partway, leave out --baud 460800.

Press RESET when it finishes. A board that uses the chip's own USB (most ESP32-S2 and S3 boards) may show up on a different port afterwards.

docs.title: Without a terminal: Thonny
docs.text:
Thonny installs MicroPython on the board through a GUI. Open Tools → Options → Interpreter and use Install or update MicroPython.

When it's done, close Thonny. Like esptool, it needs the board's port to itself.

docs.title: Other microcontrollers
docs.text:
Other chips, such as STM32, nRF or SAMD, each have their own way of installing MicroPython. See your board's page on micropython.org/download and the MicroPython documentation.

Supported hardware lists the chips Thingstudio is tested on. Another chip needs a processor definition: see Other boards.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Step 4: connect your board to Thingstudio.

docs.title: Step 5: Install the runtime
docs.text:
The runtime is the part of Thingstudio that runs on the board: it receives your flows and runs them. Each board needs it once. Libraries that a flow's nodes need are installed later, by Deploy.

  1. Check the board's port is selected in the port list, as in step 4.
  2. Choose Tools → Install runtime…. If you're connected, Thingstudio disconnects first. The console shows progress; set the console's Show menu to Info to see each file.
  3. If the board is busy and doesn't stop, the console asks you to press its reset button. On a board without one, such as a Pico, unplug it and plug it back in.
  4. The board restarts when the install is done. Click Connect. If the port has gone from the list, click ⟳ first.

After upgrading Thingstudio, the board's runtime may no longer match the editor. Deploy then stops, and the console says to install the runtime again.

If the install fails, the console says what the board sent back and what to do. See Board won't connect.

To install the runtime from the command line instead, see Command line.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Step 6: blink an LED, your first flow.

docs.title: Node conventions
docs.text: A node moves a message from one point in a flow to the next. These are the rules a custom node follows; the file format itself is in Writing custom nodes.

docs.title: The message
docs.text:
A message is a dict: msg = {'payload': ..., 'topic': ..., <anything else>}.

  • payload is the node's value. It is what the output port's declared type checks against and the one key a generic downstream node reads — debug prints only payload. Put the value you want wired and checked here.
  • topic is a routing string. Set it to a real protocol topic when the node has one, otherwise ''. Don't put the node's own event or state in topic; use a named field instead.
  • anything else rides along under its own name, and only a node written to read that name sees it.

Put one value in payload and leave the rest as named fields. The DHT22 example sends the temperature in payload and the humidity in msg['humidity'].

docs.title: Ports
docs.text: Port types are int, number, bool, string, bytes and any, the same as built-in nodes, with the same wire checks. A declared output type must match what the node puts in payload. Use any when unsure. A custom node has one input and one output: a source has the output, a sink the input.

docs.title: Kind
docs.text:
Every node is one of three kinds:

  • source — makes its own messages, on the intervalMs schedule.
  • transform — one message in, one out. Return the message, or None to stop it.
  • sink — consumes a message and produces nothing.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: A runtime error in your Python is reported from the board, attributed to your node. A transform that returns None stops that message; anything it passes on continues. The full list is under Errors in Writing custom nodes.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
A custom node has the following limits:

  • A source's emit runs on a timer, not on an external event — there are no event-driven custom sources.
  • Two instances of the same custom node get independent setup, so don't put two on the same physical resource, such as the same pin.
  • Your Python runs with the same trust as the function node. Read a package before you put it in the folder.

docs.title: Node catalog
docs.text:
Every node a flow file can use: its type id, its ports with their payload types, and its properties with the default the editor gives a new node. A property a flow file leaves out gets this default. Allowed values and ranges are checked when the flow is compiled, and the error says what is allowed. See Check a flow without the editor.

Ports are numbered from 0 in a flow file's edges: [fromNodeId, outputNumber, toNodeId, inputNumber], in the order listed here.

docs.title: change
docs.text:
Type thingstudio/change, kind transform, palette group general.

  • Inputs: msg (any)
  • Outputs: msg (any)
  • Properties (name, type, default):
    • operation, string, default "set"
    • scope, string, default "msg"
    • property, string, default "payload"
    • valueFrom, string, default "literal"
    • valueType, string, default "string"
    • value, string, default ""

docs.title: debug
docs.text:
Type thingstudio/debug, kind sink, palette group general.

  • Inputs: msg (any)
  • Outputs: none
  • Properties (name, type, default):
    • fullMessage, boolean, default false

docs.title: delay
docs.text:
Type thingstudio/delay, kind transform, palette group general.

  • Inputs: msg (any)
  • Outputs: msg (any)
  • Properties (name, type, default):
    • delayMs, number, default 1000

docs.title: filter
docs.text:
Type thingstudio/filter, kind transform, palette group general.

  • Inputs: msg (any)
  • Outputs: msg (any)
  • Properties (name, type, default):
    • mode, string, default "change"
    • threshold, number, default 1
    • intervalMs, number, default 1000
    • ignoreFirst, boolean, default false
    • perTopic, boolean, default true

docs.title: function
docs.text:
Type thingstudio/function, kind transform, palette group general.

  • Inputs: msg (any)
  • Outputs: msg (any) (the number of outputs is the node's outputCount property)
  • Properties (name, type, default):
    • code, string, default "msg['payload'] = msg['payload']\nreturn msg\n" — the body of a MicroPython function; msg in, return the message, None, or a list with one entry per output
    • outputCount, number, default 1 — how many outputs, 1 to 10

docs.title: inject
docs.text:
Type thingstudio/inject, kind source, palette group general.

  • Inputs: none
  • Outputs: msg (bool)
  • Properties (name, type, default):
    • payloadType, string, default "bool"
    • payloadValue, string, default "true"

docs.title: journal
docs.text:
Type thingstudio/journal, kind transform, palette group general.

  • Inputs: msg (any)
  • Outputs: series (any), rollup (any)
  • Properties (name, type, default):
    • rows, number, default 60 — how many rows are kept, 1 to 256
    • stepSeconds, number, default 60 — seconds per row; 0 makes every message its own row
    • steps, number, default 0 — rows per roll-up to the second output; 0 sends none
    • xff, number, default 0.5 — 0 to 1: a roll-up becomes a gap if more than this fraction of its rows are gaps

docs.title: startup
docs.text:
Type thingstudio/startup, kind source, palette group general.

  • Inputs: none
  • Outputs: msg (bool)
  • Properties (name, type, default):
    • payloadType, string, default "bool"
    • payloadValue, string, default "true"

docs.title: timer
docs.text:
Type thingstudio/timer, kind source, palette group general.

  • Inputs: none
  • Outputs: msg (int)
  • Properties (name, type, default):
    • intervalMs, number, default 1000 — milliseconds between messages; the payload is a count that rises 1, 2, 3...

docs.title: bar
docs.text:
Type thingstudio/gui_bar, kind sink, palette group GUI.

  • Inputs: msg (any)
  • Outputs: none
  • Properties (name, type, default):
    • name, string, default ""
    • style, string, default "solid"
    • segments, number, default 10
    • lo, number, default 0 — the value at which the bar is empty
    • hi, number, default 100 — the value at which the bar is full
    • staleAfter, number, default 0 — seconds without a new value before it dims; 0 = never

docs.title: button
docs.text:
Type thingstudio/gui_button, kind sink, palette group GUI.

  • Inputs: msg (any)
  • Outputs: msg (any)
  • Properties (name, type, default):
    • name, string, default ""
    • mode, string, default "momentary" — momentary, toggle or navigate
    • style, string, default "box"
    • valueType, string, default "bool" — bool, string or number: the type of what it sends
    • fireOn, string, default "release" — release (default: the finger lifts inside the button) or press
    • text, string, default "" — what is drawn on the button; empty uses name
    • value, string, default "" — momentary: what it sends; empty sends true, 'ON' or 1 by valueType
    • maxChars, number, default 8 — room for this many characters (a value replaces the text)
    • onValue, string, default "" — toggle: what it sends to turn on
    • offValue, string, default "" — toggle: what it sends to turn off
    • onText, string, default "ON"
    • offText, string, default "OFF"
    • initial, boolean, default false
    • pendingTimeout, number, default 5 — toggle with a wired input: seconds to wait for the input to confirm before going back
    • target, string, default "" — navigate: next, prev, back, home or a page name from screens

docs.text:
Type thingstudio/gui_label, kind sink, palette group GUI.

  • Inputs: msg (any)
  • Outputs: none
  • Properties (name, type, default):
    • name, string, default ""
    • maxChars, number, default 8 — room for this many characters
    • staleAfter, number, default 0 — seconds without a new value before it dims; 0 = never

docs.text:
Type thingstudio/gui_led, kind sink, palette group GUI.

  • Inputs: msg (any)
  • Outputs: none
  • Properties (name, type, default):
    • name, string, default ""
    • style, string, default "light"
    • onText, string, default "On"
    • offText, string, default "Off"
    • staleAfter, number, default 0 — seconds without a new value before it goes grey; 0 = never

docs.title: modal
docs.text:
Type thingstudio/gui_modal, kind sink, palette group GUI.

  • Inputs: msg (any)
  • Outputs: msg (any)
  • Properties (name, type, default):
    • name, string, default ""
    • screen, string, default "" — the id of the gui_screen node this modal belongs to
    • priority, number, default 0 — a higher priority takes the screen from a lower one; the other waits
    • timeout, number, default 0 — seconds before the modal closes itself; 0 never

docs.title: navigator
docs.text:
Type thingstudio/gui_navigator, kind transform, palette group GUI.

  • Inputs: msg (any)
  • Outputs: page (string)
  • Properties (name, type, default):
    • name, string, default "navigator"
    • screen, string, default ""
