docs.title: A sensor display
docs.text:
Build a three-page touch display: the room's temperature, humidity and pressure with their recent history, and a clock. The flow also publishes the readings over MQTT.

The finished flow is in the Thingstudio repository: test-flows/gui-headliner-sensor-freenove-s3-4in.flow.json. Open it in one of two ways:

  • Open the finished flow. Download it and open it with File → Open…, then set your own WiFi and MQTT credentials in its config nodes.
  • Build it yourself. Follow the steps below.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
The steps use this hardware and setup:

  • A Freenove ESP32-S3 4.0" touch display (FNK0104S), with MicroPython and the runtime installed (Getting started steps 3 to 5). Pick it by hand in the Board menu. Other boards work too; the pins below are this board's.
  • A BME280 sensor board. A BMP280 also works, without humidity. Wire it to 3V3, GND, SCL 15 and SDA 16, the touch panel's I2C bus.
  • A WiFi network for the clock and MQTT, and an MQTT broker. See Connecting over WiFi.

docs.title: 1. Read the sensor
docs.text:
1. Drag a bme280 onto the canvas. In its I2C bus field, click + and make a bus: bus 0, SCL 15, SDA 16.
  2. Set the bme280's address to 0x76, or 0x77 if your sensor board ties SDO high, and interval (ms) to 5000.

  3. Drag a function node, set outputs to 5, wire the bme280 to it, and use this code:

    p = msg['payload']
t = {'topic': 'temperature', 'payload': p['temperature']}
h = None
if p['humidity'] is not None:   # a BMP280 has no humidity
    h = {'topic': 'humidity', 'payload': p['humidity']}
pr = {'topic': 'pressure', 'payload': p['pressure']}
ok = {'topic': 'sensor', 'payload': True}
return [t, h, pr, pr, ok]

    Each reading goes out on its own output, so each widget gets only its own number. Output 4 is a second copy of the pressure, for its journal. Output 5 says the sensor is alive.

To test the sensor first, wire the bme280 to a debug node and deploy. A reading appears every 5 seconds. See bme280.

docs.title: 2. Show it on the display
docs.text:
1. Drag a display spi onto the canvas and set it for the Freenove panel:

    Property Value controller st7796 frame format rgb565 SPI bus 1 baudrate 40000000 sck, mosi, dc, cs pin 12, 11, 46, 10 reset pin -1 backlight pin 45 width, height 320, 480 rotation 1 orientation 90° clockwise color order BGR invert colors, data latch order on

    Click 💾 to save these as a preset for next time. 2. Drag a gui screen. Set its width and height to the panel's own size, 320 and 480, and its frame format to rgb565. Wire it to the display spi. 3. In the gui screen's touch panel field, click + and make a Touch panel: controller FT6336U, the same I2C bus, address 0x38, width 320, height 480. 4. Drag three gui readout nodes (temperature, humidity, pressure) and a gui light for the sensor. Wire the function's outputs 1, 2, 3 and 5 to them. In each readout, set units, decimals, lowest value and highest value. 5. Lay out the pages: select the gui screen and use the page outline in its properties to add rows of text and readouts. See Laying out pages.

Set stale after on the readouts and the light. A reading that stops arriving is then dimmed, so a dead sensor looks different from a steady room.

docs.title: 3. Add the history
docs.text:
A journal keeps the recent readings, and a gui trend draws them.

  1. Wire the temperature output to a journal with seconds per row 10, rows kept 156 and rows per roll-up 6. Wire its first output to a gui trend. That trend shows the last 26 minutes.
  2. Wire the journal's second output, one summary per minute, to a second journal with seconds per row 0. Wire that journal to a second gui trend, which shows the last 2.6 hours.
  3. Wire output 4, the pressure copy, to a journal with seconds per row 60, and that to a third gui trend.

Each bar is the average of its row, and the thin line runs from the row's min to its max. Set each trend's bottom at and top at to the range you expect, for example 15 to 30 for temperature. See Trend.

docs.title: 4. Add the clock
docs.text:
1. Drag a timer with interval (ms) 1000, and two ntp nodes. Wire the timer to both.
  2. Set one ntp node's format to time and the other's to date. In both, set UTC offset (hours) for your zone's standard time, and daylight saving to UK / EU: automatic if that's where you are, otherwise none. See ntp.
  3. Add two gui label nodes, one for the time with room for (characters) 5, and one for the date with 10. Wire the time ntp node to the first and the date one to the second.
  4. On a new page, give the time label the font font_seg764 (seven-segment digits) and the date font_body24.

Until the board has the time, the labels show --.

docs.title: 5. Turn the pages
docs.text:
Add a gui button with mode navigate to each page, so you can turn the pages by touch. See Buttons.

The example flow also turns the pages every 8 seconds with a gui navigator node, which isn't in the palette. See GUI nodes.

docs.title: 6. Publish the readings
docs.text: Drag three mqtt publish nodes, one per reading, with topics such as thingstudio/headliner/temperature. Wire outputs 1 to 3 of the function to them, and pick your MQTT broker and WiFi. See mqtt publish.

docs.title: Deploy
docs.text: Click Compile → Deploy. The display lights, the readings appear within 5 seconds, the trends fill as the minutes pass, and the clock starts once the board has the time.

docs.title: If it doesn't work
docs.text:
Each symptom below has its own fix:

  • The picture is scrambled: the width and height on both the gui screen and the display spi must be the panel's own size, 320 and 480, even when the picture is turned. Deploy checks this and says so.
  • Touches land in the wrong place: see Touch panels.
  • No readings: check the wiring and the address (0x76 or 0x77), and test with a debug node.
  • The clock stays at --: the ntp node's status says why: no WiFi yet, or the NTP server can't be reached. It tries again every 30 seconds.
  • Compile says a node is "disconnected from any source": a widget has nothing wired to it. Wire it, or reload the editor if the wires are there.

docs.title: Other boards
docs.text:
Other boards that run MicroPython may work. Thingstudio needs a processor definition for the chip, and a board definition if you want the board's own pins labelled. See Adding a board and Adding a processor.

An AI assistant can draft a definition file. Give it the board's pinout or the chip's datasheet, and one of the existing files in ~/.thingstudio/boards/ or ~/.thingstudio/processors/ as an example. Check the result against the datasheet. A missing reserved pin means the compile won't stop a flow that crashes the board.

docs.title: Reporting hardware
docs.text:
Reports on any board, display or sensor, listed or not, are welcome. Open an issue on GitHub with:

  • the board, processor and any display or sensor
  • the MicroPython version
  • what worked and what didn't

A definition file for a new board can be attached to the issue.

docs.title: The Thingstudio folder
docs.text:
Thingstudio keeps its own files in one folder on your computer:

  • macOS and Linux: ~/.thingstudio
  • Windows: %USERPROFILE%\.thingstudio

Thingstudio creates the folder the first time it starts. Your flows are not kept here. They are saved wherever you choose (see Flow lifecycle).

docs.title: What's in it
docs.text:
Folder Holds Edit by hand? credentials/ WiFi and MQTT broker logins, saved by name No, use the editor presets/ Saved node settings, one folder per node type Yes custom-nodes/ Your own node types Yes boards/ Board definitions Yes processors/ Processor definitions Yes

Every file is plain JSON, except the .node.py file of a custom node. The editor reads these folders through the Thingstudio backend, so they aren't available when the editor talks to the board directly over USB.

docs.title: Credentials
docs.text:
A WiFi or MQTT broker config node holds only the name of a credential. The SSID, password, broker address and login are stored in credentials/wifi/<name>.json or credentials/mqtt-broker/<name>.json. This keeps secrets out of flow files you share or commit. Create and edit credentials from the config node (see Config nodes).

The files are not encrypted. Anyone who can read your home folder can read them. Don't commit this folder or copy it to shared storage.

docs.title: Presets
docs.text: A preset is a named set of property values for one node type, such as the pins and size of a display panel. You save and load presets from a node's property panel (see Presets). Each one is a file at presets/<node type>/<name>.json. A file that isn't valid JSON appears in the list disabled, with the file named.

docs.title: Custom nodes
docs.text: A custom node is two files with the same base name: <name>.node.json and <name>.node.py. The first time Thingstudio starts, it puts two examples here. Deleted examples don't come back. See Custom nodes.

docs.title: Boards and processors
docs.text:
At every start, Thingstudio copies any built-in definition that's missing from boards/ and processors/. It never overwrites a file that's already there.

  • To change a built-in, edit its file.
  • To get the original back, delete the file and restart Thingstudio.
  • After an upgrade, an existing copy still wins over a changed built-in, until you delete it.

See Boards and processors.

docs.title: Using a different folder
docs.text:
Start Thingstudio with --data-dir:

thingstudio --data-dir ~/projects/greenhouse/thingstudio-data

This keeps separate sets of credentials, presets and custom nodes, for example one per project.

docs.title: Connecting over WiFi
docs.text: The editor can connect to a board over WiFi instead of USB. Once connected over WiFi, everything works the same as over USB: deploy, the console, Tools → Check status, and clicking an inject node.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A board with WiFi and the Thingstudio runtime. Plain Raspberry Pi Pico and Pico 2 boards have no WiFi.
  • A flow on the board that uses WiFi and has joined your network. The board is only reachable while that flow is running. It starts again by itself after a reset.
  • A board password, set over USB.
  • This computer on the same network as the board.
  • On a Mac, Thingstudio started from Apple's Terminal app. See If it doesn't connect.

docs.title: Set the password and name
docs.text:
1. Connect the board over USB.
  2. Choose Tools → Board settings…. The top line names the board these settings apply to: its chip, USB port and current name.
  3. Enter a network name and a password of 8 to 64 characters, then click Save to board.

The name and password are stored on the board, not in the flow. The editor also remembers the password on this computer. A board with no password only accepts USB.

A new name is used from the next time the board joins WiFi. Reset the board to use it straight away.

docs.title: Connect
docs.text:
Click ⟳ next to the port list. Boards on your network appear in the port menu under WiFi. Pick one and click Connect.

If the board isn't listed, choose WiFi address… and type its name (for example kitchen or kitchen.local) or its IP address.

If this computer has no saved password for the board, the editor asks for it.

A board with no password is listed as no password set. It won't accept a WiFi connection until you set one.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• Only one editor can connect over WiFi at a time.
  • Board settings can only be changed over USB.
  • Installing the runtime and Tools → Remove flow… need USB.
  • If the board loses power or leaves WiFi range, the editor shows it disconnected within about 30 seconds.
  • Deploying a flow that doesn't use WiFi takes the board off the network at its next reset.
  • The password is never sent over the network, but the connection isn't encrypted. Use it on a network you trust.

docs.title: If it doesn't connect
docs.text:
The console says what went wrong:

  • No route to host (Mac): macOS is blocking local network access. The first time Thingstudio reaches for the network, macOS asks whether it may find devices on your local network; choose Allow, then click Connect again (the attempt that raised the question can fail). If you chose Don't Allow, turn thingstudio-python on in System Settings → Privacy & Security → Local Network, then restart Thingstudio. When running from source (thingstudio-backend), macOS may block it without asking: start it from Apple's Terminal app instead, which macOS always allows.
  • No answer: check the board is on, its flow has joined WiFi, and this computer is on the same network. If a .local name doesn't work, try the IP address, shown in the console when you connect over USB.
  • Wrong password: the editor asks again. To change it, connect over USB and use Tools → Board settings….
  • Already has a network session: another editor is connected. Disconnect it first.
  • No password set or Connection refused: the board has no password, so it only accepts USB. Set one over USB in Tools → Board settings…, then click ⟳.
  • Board not listed: click ⟳ again. If it's still missing, check its flow has joined WiFi, or use WiFi address…. If the console says the WiFi scan didn't run, the reason follows; on a Mac it's usually the Local Network permission (see No route to host above).

docs.title: WiFi provisioning
docs.text: You can leave a flow's WiFi network and password out, and enter them on the board when it first starts. Use this for a board you hand to someone else, or one that goes on a network you don't have the password for.

docs.title: Turning it on
docs.text: In the flow's WiFi config, set security to Unmanaged and leave the credential blank. See Config nodes. Deploy as usual.

docs.title: Entering the network on the board
docs.text:
When the board starts with no saved network, it opens its own WiFi network, Thingstudio-Setup-XXXX, with the password thingstudio:

  1. Connect a phone or laptop to Thingstudio-Setup-XXXX. Most phones open the setup page by themselves. If not, browse to http://192.168.4.1/.
  2. Pick your network from the list, or type its name. Some boards' scans miss nearby networks, so typing always works.
  3. Enter the password and submit.

Once the board connects, it saves the network and joins it on every later start. If nobody enters a network within 10 minutes, the board carries on starting without WiFi.

docs.title: Reopening setup when WiFi fails
docs.text:
By default, setup only runs while no network is saved. If the saved network later becomes unreachable, the board stays disconnected.

Tick Allow reprovisioning on connect failure in the WiFi config to reopen the setup network whenever the saved network fails. Only do this on a network you control: while the setup network is open, anyone in range who knows its password can point the board at a different network.

docs.title: Changing the setup network's password
docs.text:
There's no field for it in the editor. Connect to the board and type this in the command box under the console (see Commands and the Python prompt):

import wifi_provision; wifi_provision.set_ap_password('yournewpassword')

Then choose Tools → Reset board (hard). Use at least 8 characters: with fewer, the setup network doesn't open. Set it to 'thingstudio' to go back to the default.

docs.title: Starting over
docs.text:
To make the board forget its saved network and run setup again, type this in the command box, then reset the board:

import os; os.remove('/_wifi_provision.json')

This also clears a changed setup password.

docs.title: Editor in depth
docs.text: How the editor's wiring, node labels, presets, config nodes and node status work.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Every port has a type: int, number, bool, string, bytes or any. The editor refuses a wire between types that don't fit. What each input type accepts:

Input Accepts wires from any any output bool any output. The value is tested with Python's bool(). number number, int, string int int, string string string bytes bytes, any

A string that isn't a number fails on the board when it reaches a number or int input, with a NODE_ERROR. An any output, such as the output of a function node, connects only to any, bool and bytes inputs.

An input can take any number of wires. The node runs once for each message that arrives, whichever wire it came on. An output can feed any number of inputs.

docs.title: Giving a node a flow label
docs.text:
Every node has a flow label field at the top of its property panel. Type something, say Fire!, and the canvas shows it instead of the node's name. Leave it blank to show the name again. Console messages and errors that name the node use the flow label too.

A gui button also has a board label, the text drawn on the button. If the board label is blank, the button shows the flow label.

docs.title: Presets
docs.text:
A preset is a named set of property values, such as the pins and size of one display panel. display spi, display i2c and the Touch panel config have a preset menu at the top of their property panel:

  • Pick a preset to copy its values into the node's properties.
  • Click 💾 to save the current values as a preset, under a name you choose.
  • Click ↻ to read the preset files again.

Applying a preset copies the values once. Later changes to the node or the preset don't affect each other.

Each preset is a JSON file in ~/.thingstudio/presets/<node type>/, which you can also write by hand. A file that isn't valid JSON appears in the menu disabled, with the file named. See The Thingstudio folder.

docs.title: Config nodes
docs.text:
A config node holds settings that several nodes share. A node's property panel has a field to pick one; ✎ edits it and + makes a new one. The config nodes are:

  • WiFi: a saved credential and a security mode: password, open, or unmanaged.
  • MQTT Broker: a saved credential holding the host, port and optional username and password.
  • I2C bus: the bus number, SCL and SDA pins, and frequency. See I2C bus.
  • Touch panel: the touch controller, its I2C bus and address, and its size and orientation. See Touch panels.

The WiFi and MQTT Broker configs hold only the name of a saved credential. The SSID, passwords and broker address are saved by name in ~/.thingstudio/credentials/, not in the flow file, so a flow you share or commit holds no secrets. Two flows that use the same credential share its values: edit it once and both change. Pick, edit or add a credential from the config's credential field. See The Thingstudio folder.

A flow has one WiFi network. Every node that uses WiFi has a WiFi field, and they all show the same setting: change it on one and it changes on all. A flow doesn't need a wifi status node to use the network.

docs.title: Node status
docs.text:
Some nodes show a colored dot and a line of text under the node while the editor is connected to the board:

Dot Meaning Green connected Amber connecting Gray disconnected Red error

The dot shows what the board reports, not the editor's guess. It appears once the running flow first reports, and clears on every deploy until the new flow reports.

The nodes with a status are wifi status, mqtt publish, mqtt subscribe, i2c device, bme280, touch, and a gui screen with a touch panel.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: The Notes panel on the right is free text about the flow: what it does, what to wire up, how to use it. It's saved in the flow file, and opens by itself when you open a flow that has notes. File → New flow clears it.

docs.title: Event-driven programming
docs.text: An event-driven program waits for things to happen, and runs a piece of code for each one. A button press, a timer tick and an incoming network message are all events. The code that handles one is often called a handler.

docs.title: The loop you may know
docs.text:
Most microcontroller programs start as a loop:

while True:
    if button.value() == 0:
        led.on()
    temperature = sensor.read()
    time.sleep(0.1)

Every job lives inside the loop, and each one waits for the others. A slow sensor read delays the button check. A sleep long enough to pace one job stalls all of them. Adding a job means reworking the timing of the rest.

docs.title: The same program, as events
docs.text:
Written as events, each job stands on its own:

  • when the button pin falls, turn the LED on
  • every 10 seconds, read the sensor

Nothing is checked in a loop. The board sleeps until an event arrives, runs its handler, and waits again. Jobs with different timing don't get in each other's way.

docs.title: How Thingstudio does it
docs.text:
Thingstudio is built on asyncio, MicroPython's built-in module for event-driven programming. It provides an event loop: one scheduler that runs many tasks, switching between them whenever one is waiting.

In Thingstudio, each chain of nodes that starts at a source (a timer, an interrupt, an mqtt subscribe) is one handler. When you deploy, the flow is turned into MicroPython code in which each source becomes an asyncio task. While one task waits, for a timer or the network, the others run.

docs.title: The one rule: don't block
docs.text:
Everything shares one event loop. A handler that stops and waits without handing control back stops every other handler too. In a function node, that means no time.sleep() and no long loops.

To wait, use a node built for it: delay waits, timer repeats. They hand control back while they wait. Inside a function node, await asyncio.sleep(1) does the same:

await asyncio.sleep(1)
return msg

docs.title: More
docs.text:
Further reading:

  • MicroPython's asyncio
  • Peter Hinch's asyncio tutorial for MicroPython

docs.title: Flows, nodes and messages
docs.text: A Thingstudio program is a flow: a set of nodes joined by wires. You build it by dragging nodes onto a canvas and wiring them together, rather than writing a program top to bottom.

docs.title: Nodes
docs.text:
A node does one job. Most fall into three kinds:

  • Sources start things off: timer fires on an interval, interrupt fires when a pin changes, mqtt subscribe fires when a message arrives.
  • Transforms change or filter what passes through: function, filter, delay.
  • Sinks do something at the end: gpio out switches a pin, display spi draws, mqtt publish sends.

Each node has properties, set in the editor's property panel: a pin number, an interval, a topic.

docs.title: Messages
docs.text:
Nodes pass messages along wires. A message is a Python dict with two standard keys:

  • payload: the main value, such as a reading, a count or a string
  • topic: a short label saying what the message is about
{'payload': 21.5, 'topic': 'kitchen/temperature'}

Nodes may add other keys. A node reads the ones it needs and passes the rest on.

docs.title: Wires
docs.text:
A wire joins an output to an input. One output can feed several inputs, and each gets its own copy of the message. Several outputs can feed one input, and the node runs once per message, whichever wire it came in on.

Each port has a type, such as int, number, bool, string or any. The editor refuses a wire between ports whose types don't fit.

docs.title: Config nodes
docs.text: Settings that several nodes share, like a WiFi network or an MQTT broker, live in a config node. You set it up once and pick it from each node that uses it. See Editor in depth.

docs.title: Background
docs.text: Node-and-wire programming has a long history, from J. Paul Morrison's flow-based programming to tools like LabVIEW, Max and Node-RED. Thingstudio follows Node-RED's version of the idea, with the same message shape and very similar nodes.

docs.title: MicroPython
docs.text: MicroPython is a version of Python 3 made to run on microcontrollers. It fits in hundreds of kilobytes and runs directly on the chip, with no operating system underneath.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
You flash MicroPython onto the board once, like any firmware. After that the board runs Python files from its own filesystem, and gives you a Python prompt, the REPL, over USB. You can type Python at the board and see the result at once.

MicroPython keeps most of the Python language and part of its standard library. It adds modules for hardware: machine for pins, I2C, SPI and PWM, network for WiFi, and asyncio for running several tasks at once.

from machine import Pin
led = Pin(15, Pin.OUT)
led.on()

docs.title: The limits
docs.text: Microcontrollers are limited. A board typically has hundreds of kilobytes of RAM, and MicroPython itself uses some of it. Python is also much slower than C, though fast enough for most sensing, switching and networking jobs.

docs.title: Where Thingstudio fits
docs.text:
Thingstudio runs on top of MicroPython. It installs a runtime onto the board, and turns each flow you deploy into MicroPython code. The function node runs your own MicroPython. See installing MicroPython to get it onto your board.

If you already use MicroPython, see if you know MicroPython for how Thingstudio uses your board.

docs.title: More
docs.text:
Further reading:

  • MicroPython documentation
  • MicroPython quick reference for ESP32 and for RP2

docs.title: Node-RED
docs.text: Node-RED is a free tool for wiring together devices, web services and APIs. You build programs, called flows, in a browser by dragging nodes onto a canvas and wiring them up. It was created at IBM in 2013 and is now an OpenJS Foundation project.

docs.title: What people use it for
docs.text: Node-RED is popular for home automation and IoT. A typical flow might take sensor readings from MQTT, check them, store them in a database and send an alert when something is out of range. It has thousands of add-on nodes and a dashboard for building web UIs.

docs.title: Where it runs
docs.text: Node-RED runs on Node.js, on a server, a PC or a Raspberry Pi. Microcontrollers usually talk to it over the network, often by MQTT, and run their own separate firmware.

docs.title: Where Thingstudio fits
docs.text:
Thingstudio takes Node-RED's way of working onto the microcontroller. The flow runs on the board itself, so the board doesn't need a server to decide what to do. The two work well together: a Thingstudio board can publish readings over MQTT to a Node-RED flow on your server.

If you already use Node-RED, see if you know Node-RED for what's different.

docs.title: More
docs.text:
Further reading:

  • Node-RED concepts
  • Node-RED getting started

docs.title: If you know Arduino and C
docs.text: If you've written setup() and loop() in C or C++, Thingstudio will feel different in three ways. It uses Python rather than C, you wire events together instead of writing a loop, and a change goes to the board in seconds without reflashing.

docs.title: Python instead of C
docs.text:
The board runs MicroPython, which you flash once in place of an Arduino sketch. Your own code, in function nodes and custom nodes, is Python.

Python is slower than C and uses more memory. That's fine for sensing, switching, displays and networking. It's the wrong tool for tight timing, such as bit-banging a protocol at microsecond precision or sampling at high rates.

docs.title: Events instead of a loop
docs.text:
There's no loop(). Each job is its own chain of nodes, started by an event: a timer, a pin change, a network message. Jobs don't wait for each other. See event-driven programming.

The interrupt node works like attachInterrupt(). The difference is that your code runs safely in the main program, not inside the interrupt, so you can do anything there.

docs.title: No compile-and-flash cycle
docs.text: The firmware stays the same. Deploying a flow sends a compiled file to the board, over USB or WiFi, and the board swaps it in. Changing a flow and trying it again takes seconds.

docs.title: What stays the same
docs.text:
Thingstudio checks your pin numbers against the board before deploying, and refuses pins that would crash it, such as those wired to the flash chip. See boards and processors.

Next: getting started.

docs.title: If you know MicroPython
docs.text: Thingstudio sits on top of the MicroPython you already have. It doesn't replace your firmware. It adds a runtime and a way to write programs as flows, while the REPL and your own Python stay within reach.

docs.title: What goes on the board
docs.text:
Tools → Install runtime… copies a set of Python files onto the board's filesystem, including a main.py that starts the Thingstudio runtime at boot. The runtime listens on USB or WiFi for the editor, and runs the last flow you deployed.

If your board already has a main.py of your own, copy it off first.

docs.title: What a flow becomes
docs.text:
When you deploy, the editor turns the flow into MicroPython source. Each source node, such as a timer or an interrupt, becomes an asyncio task. The other nodes become async functions that each task calls in turn. The editor compiles the result to .mpy bytecode with mpy-cross and sends it to the board, which swaps it in without a reset. Compiling on your computer means the board never needs RAM for the compiler.

The board saves the flow and runs it again after a restart.

docs.title: Your own code
docs.text:
• Function nodes run your Python on each message. They're called from the event loop, so don't block: no time.sleep(), no long loops. See event-driven programming.
  • Custom nodes turn your own code, such as a sensor driver, into a node with its own properties. See writing custom nodes.

docs.title: The REPL
docs.text: The command box under the editor's console runs Python on the board while the flow runs, for checks like gc.mem_free(). For the full >>> prompt, click Stop flow & open prompt. To use Thonny or mpremote, click Disconnect first. See commands and the Python prompt.

docs.title: Memory
docs.text:
A flow, its nodes and the runtime all share the board's RAM. If a deploy fails for lack of space, the console says so. See debugging.

Next: getting started.

docs.title: If you know Node-RED
docs.text: Most of what you know carries over. You drag nodes onto a canvas, wire them, set properties and click Deploy. Messages carry payload and topic. Config nodes hold shared settings like an MQTT broker. The differences come from where the flow runs: on a microcontroller, not on a server.

docs.title: Where the flow runs
docs.text: The editor runs on your computer, but the flow runs on the board. Deploy compiles the flow to MicroPython and sends it to the board, which then runs on its own. Close the editor, unplug the USB cable, and the flow carries on.

docs.title: Function nodes are Python
docs.text:
Function nodes run MicroPython, not JavaScript. A message is a Python dict, so write msg['payload'], not msg.payload.

if msg['payload'] > 30:
    msg['topic'] = 'alarm'
    return msg

Much else is the same. return msg passes the message on, and returning nothing stops it. Return a list to route to several outputs. context.get()/context.set() and flow.get()/flow.set() work as you'd expect. There's no global, since there's only one flow. See the function node.

Don't use time.sleep() in a function node. It stops the whole board, not only that node. Use await asyncio.sleep() or a delay node instead. See event-driven programming.

docs.title: Messages
docs.text: Every message needs a topic, even an empty one (''). Ports also have types, such as int, bool and string, and the editor refuses a wire between types that don't fit. See Editor in depth.

docs.title: Nodes
docs.text:
The palette is smaller, and made for hardware. timer, interrupt, gpio out, pwm out and the sensor and display nodes work with the board directly. inject, debug, function, delay, mqtt, http and udp will look familiar.

You add node types by writing a JSON file and a Python file. See writing custom nodes.

docs.title: Debugging
docs.text: debug output appears in the editor's console, not a sidebar. An error in one node is reported in the console, saying which node, and the rest of the flow keeps running. See debugging.

docs.title: Using both
docs.text:
Node-RED is the better place for dashboards, databases and cloud services. A common setup is Thingstudio boards publishing over MQTT to a Node-RED flow on a server or Raspberry Pi.

Next: getting started.

docs.title: Node reference
docs.text: Every built-in node has its own page, covering what it does, its properties and its output. This page lists them all, grouped as in the editor's palette: General, Network and Hardware.

docs.title: Kinds of node
docs.text:
Each node is one of three kinds. The kind decides where it can sit in a flow.

  • Source: starts a message. Has no input. Every chain in a flow begins with one.
  • Transform: takes a message in, and passes it on, changed, delayed or not at all.
  • Sink: takes a message in and acts on it. Has no output.

See flows, nodes and messages for how they fit together.

docs.title: Which node do I need?
docs.text: To… Use do something at a fixed interval timer do something once, when the flow starts startup send a test message by hand inject respond to a pin changing interrupt, eswitch respond to presses, long presses and double clicks ebutton read an analog input adc read a rotary knob encoder drive an LED strip neopixel switch an LED or relay gpio out dim an LED or set a motor's speed pwm out read a temperature, humidity or pressure sensor bme280 talk to another I2C device, or find its address i2c device draw on a display display spi, display i2c show readings as pages on a display GUI nodes change a message, or decide where it goes function set or clear a value between messages change send only changes, or limit the rate filter keep a number's history and show its trend journal show the time of day ntp wait before passing a message on delay see what's in a message debug send or receive MQTT messages mqtt publish, mqtt subscribe call a web API http request serve a web page or API from the board http in and http response send or receive UDP packets udp send, udp receive know when WiFi connects or drops wifi status stop messages while WiFi is down wifi gate

docs.title: General
docs.text:
Nodes that don't need a network or hardware:

Node Kind What it does inject source Sends one message with a fixed payload when you click it in the editor. startup source Sends one message each time the flow starts. timer source Sends a rising count at a fixed interval. function transform Runs your own MicroPython on each message. delay transform Passes each message on after a set wait. filter transform Passes a message on only if it changed enough, or enough time has passed. change transform Sets or deletes one message property or flow variable. journal transform Keeps the recent history of a number as average, min and max rows, for a trend. debug sink Prints a message to the editor's console.

docs.title: Network
docs.text:
These nodes share the flow's WiFi network. A flow has one, set on any WiFi node's WiFi field.

Node Kind What it does wifi status source Reports when the WiFi connection comes up or goes down. wifi gate transform Passes a message on only while WiFi is connected. ntp in and out Sets the board's clock from the internet and sends the time. mqtt subscribe source Sends a message for each MQTT message on a topic. mqtt publish sink Publishes a message's payload to an MQTT topic. http request transform Makes an HTTP request per message and passes on the response. http in source Serves HTTP from the board, sending a message for each request. http response sink Answers a request that arrived through http in. udp receive source Sends a message for each UDP packet received on a port. udp send sink Sends a message's payload as a UDP packet.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text:
Pin numbers are checked against your board before a deploy. See boards and processors.

Node Kind What it does interrupt source Fires the moment a pin changes. eswitch source Reports a debounced switch opening or closing. ebutton source Reports presses, releases, long presses and double clicks. adc source Reads an analog pin, sending when the reading moves past its bounds. encoder source Reports a rotary knob's value as it turns. neopixel sink Lights a WS2812 / NeoPixel strip. gpio out sink Sets a pin high or low. pwm out sink Drives a pin with a variable duty cycle. bme280 source Reads a BME280 or BMP280 sensor at a fixed interval. i2c device transform Reads, writes or scans an I2C device that has no node of its own. display spi sink Sends a frame to an SPI color display (ST7789). display i2c sink Sends a frame to an I2C OLED display (SSD1306).

docs.title: Hardware is shared
docs.text:
Each pin, PWM output, I2C bus and SPI bus is set up once, and every node that uses it shares that one setup. Two nodes can use the same pin only if they set it up the same way. For example, an interrupt and an eswitch can both read an input pin with no pull, but a gpio out can't drive a pin an eswitch reads. When two nodes clash, the compile stops and names both.

A function or custom node gets the same objects with runtime.shared(), for example runtime.shared('i2c', 0).

docs.title: Shared settings
docs.text:
Some settings are set once and shared by the nodes that use them:

  • WiFi network and MQTT broker: config nodes, with the real passwords kept outside the flow file. See config nodes.
  • I2C bus: the pins and clock for a bus, shared by every I2C node on it. See I2C bus.
  • Touch panel: the controller, bus and size of a touch screen, used by a gui screen or a touch node. See touch panels.

docs.title: Something missing?
docs.text: A function node covers most gaps: a comparison, a sum, a calculation on a reading. For something you'll use again, write a custom node.

docs.title: adc
docs.text: Reads an ADC pin and sends a message when the reading moves outside (or back inside) the set bounds, and on a poll interval if one is set. Pin numbers are checked against your board.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• pin — the ADC pin. On ESP32 an ADC2 pin can't be used while WiFi is up, so Deploy refuses one when the flow also uses the network.
  • mode — relative (the reading moved by delta since the last message) or absolute (lower..upper).
  • delta — for relative. The smallest change that sends a message.
  • lower / upper — for absolute.
  • sense — outside (send when the reading leaves the bounds) or inside (send when it returns to them).
  • poll (ms) — also send at least this often; 0 sends only on a bounds crossing.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Output — one reading:

msg = {'payload': {'raw': 0, 'volts': 0.0, 'percent': 0.0}, 'topic': ''}

raw is the 16-bit reading (0–65535), volts the pin voltage, and percent 0–100 of the full range.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
The reading is noisy, so relative mode with a few thousand counts is the common setup; absolute suits an alarm or a threshold. With inside, a message arrives when the reading comes back within the bounds, so a flow can see both leaving and returning.

Two adc nodes on the same pin share one channel, so they must have the same settings, or the compile stops. See Hardware is shared.

docs.title: bme280
docs.text: Reads a BME280 or BMP280 temperature, humidity and pressure sensor at a fixed interval. Supported hardware lists the chips.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• I2C bus — the bus the sensor is wired to. See I2C bus.
  • address — 0x76 (most boards) or 0x77.
  • interval (ms) — how often to read. At least 100.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Output — one reading per interval:

msg = {'payload': {'temperature': 21.43, 'humidity': 48.2, 'pressure': 1012.6}, 'topic': ''}

Temperature is in °C, humidity in %, pressure in hPa. On a BMP280, humidity is None.

To use one reading, pick it out in a function node: msg['payload'] = msg['payload']['temperature'].

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text: The status dot shows whether the sensor is answering. The node tries again at the next interval, and picks up a sensor connected after the flow starts.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
If a read fails, the node sends nothing and the dot says why:

  • disconnected, no reply at 0x76 on I2C bus 0 — nothing answered. Check the wiring, pins and address.
  • error, no BME280/BMP280 at 0x76 (chip id 0x..) — a different chip is at that address.

docs.title: change
docs.text:
Sets or deletes one value on each message, then passes the message on.

Use it to hold a value between messages (a last reading, a counter set elsewhere) or to copy one into a message. It is the no-code way to work with the flow store that a function node's flow.get/flow.set uses.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• operation — set or delete.
  • target — msg property or flow variable.
  • property / name — the message property or flow variable to change.
  • value from (set only) — a literal value, another msg property, or a flow variable.
  • literal type (set from a literal) — string, number or bool.
  • value / source property — the literal, or the name of the message property / flow variable to copy.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
One rule per node. Chain change nodes for more than one change.

A flow variable is shared by name across the whole flow: another change node and a function node using flow.get/flow.set see the same value. Flow variables are in RAM and are cleared when the flow is redeployed.

Node context is not offered here; use a function node for a value private to that one node.

inject "hello" → change (flow.last = msg.payload) → change (msg.payload = flow.last) → debug

The second node reads the value the first one stored, and the debug node prints hello.

docs.title: debug
docs.text: Prints a message's payload to the device's console — the way to see what's actually flowing through a wire.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text: • full message — off by default. Prints the whole message (topic, and any other fields a source node adds — for example wifi status's ip/subnet/gateway/dns/rssi) instead of only payload.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text: Output goes to the device's serial console, visible in the editor's console panel once connected. Use it to see a value flowing through a wire without guessing.

docs.title: delay
docs.text: Passes a message through unchanged, after waiting a configured interval.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text: • delay (ms) — how long to hold the message before releasing it. Must be a positive number.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text: The wait blocks the message's own source, not only this one message. A timer node ticking every 200ms feeding a delay of 5000ms stops ticking every 200ms once a message reaches the delay: the timer's next tick can't fire until the whole chain, including the delay, finishes. Any slow node has the same effect on its own source, but delay's entire job is waiting, so it pays to know this up front.

docs.title: display i2c
docs.text:
Pushes an already-rendered frame to an I2C mono OLED panel. The controller property selects the display chip; Supported hardware lists it. Build the frame upstream (a function node using framebuf.FrameBuffer) and wire it into this node's input.

This node's property panel has a preset picker (see Editor in depth) — save a real panel's pin/address setup under a name once, then load it again on this or another display i2c node instead of retyping it.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• controller — the display chip. SSD1306.
  • I2C bus — the bus the panel is wired to. See I2C bus.
  • address — the I2C address, addr in the flow file, as a plain number: 60 is 0x3C, the usual SSD1306 address.
  • width / height — panel resolution in pixels. Height must be a multiple of 8.

A flow saved before I2C buses existed has its pins on the node. The editor moves them into an I2C bus when it opens the flow. Save the flow to keep the change.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text: Input — a raw MONO_VLSB-encoded buffer, exactly width * (height / 8) bytes, the same format framebuf.FrameBuffer produces for a 1-bit surface. A wrong-length buffer raises a clear error rather than silently corrupting the display's internal buffer indexing.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text: Only I2C wiring is supported — an SSD1306 wired over SPI isn't covered by this node. No drawing primitives here: this node only pushes a complete, already-rendered frame on every message.

docs.title: Text on the panel
docs.text:
Draw in a function node with framebuf (an import inside the function body works) and send the buffer, not the FrameBuffer object. fb.text() uses a fixed 8x8 font, so a 128x64 panel holds 16 characters on each of 8 lines. The node accepts bytearray or bytes. A panel sharing a bus with a sensor such as a BME280 works at the bus's one speed; the default is fine for both.

import framebuf
buf = context.get('buf')
if buf is None:
    buf = bytearray(128 * 8)
    context.set('buf', buf)
fb = framebuf.FrameBuffer(buf, 128, 64, framebuf.MONO_VLSB)
fb.fill(0)
fb.text('%.1f C' % msg['payload']['temperature'], 0, 28, 1)
msg['payload'] = buf
return msg

docs.title: display spi
docs.text:
Pushes an already-rendered frame to an SPI color TFT panel. Supported hardware lists the display chips. Build the frame upstream (a function node using framebuf.FrameBuffer) and wire it into this node's input.

This node's property panel has a preset picker (see Editor in depth) — save a real panel's whole setup (pins, bus, resolution, rotation, color order, and so on) under a name once, then load it again on this or another display spi node instead of retyping every field.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• controller — the display chip. See Supported hardware.
  • frame format — rgb565 (default, full color, width * height * 2 bytes), or an indexed format: gs4 (4-bit, a quarter the memory), gs2 (2-bit, an eighth), or mono (1-bit, a sixteenth). Switch away from rgb565 if a full buffer won't fit in memory; the lower the depth, the smaller the buffer, at the cost of fewer colors. The gui screen wired to the display uses this format.
  • palette — 16 RGB565 colors, used by every indexed format (gs4 reads all 16, gs2 only the first 4, mono only the first 2). Shown as swatches under frame format when an indexed format is picked; click one to change it, or reset for the built-in colors. Colors are rounded to the nearest the panel can show.
  • SPI bus — which hardware SPI peripheral to use. Default 2.
  • baudrate — SPI clock speed. Default 40MHz. On an ESP32, use 27MHz or less unless sck and mosi are the bus's fast pins; the compile tells you if the speed is too high for your board.
  • sck / mosi / dc pins — required GPIO pins, checked against your board.
  • cs / reset / backlight pins — optional GPIO pins (−1 for "not wired"). Some boards tie reset or CS high in hardware, or have no backlight control at all.
  • width / height — panel resolution in pixels. The gui screen wired to the display takes this size.
  • orientation — off by default. Set it to 0, 90, 180 or 270 to turn the picture clockwise; the gui screen wired to the display and its touch follow. With an orientation, set width and height to the panel's own size, rotation to how the panel is mounted (0 to 3), and xstart/ystart to -1. See Rotating the screen. A flow that reads touch with a touch node rather than a gui screen sets the same angle on that node.
  • palette — the colours an indexed frame format uses. While a gui screen with a theme is wired to this display, the theme supplies the palette and this one is ignored.
  • rotation — 0–7, the panel controller's orientation code. Default 1.
  • color order — rgb or bgr, matching your panel's own wiring. Default bgr.
  • invert colors — on or off. Some panels need this flipped to show true colors instead of their negative.
  • data latch order — on or off, a separate controller bit (MH) some panels need alongside rotation for correct left-right orientation.
  • xstart / ystart — the panel's offset into the ST7789 controller's own (larger) frame memory (GRAM). Default -1 resolves it from the driver's built-in table for the two panel sizes it knows (240×240 → 0, 0; 135×240 → 52, 40). Any other resolution needs both set explicitly, or the driver raises an error at flow-boot time. Getting it wrong doesn't error: it blits into the wrong window of GRAM, so content shows up clipped or offset. An ST7796 panel has no offset: leave both at -1.

Pins, bus, resolution, rotation, color order, inversion and data latch order vary board to board — there's no sensible default that works for more than one board, so confirm these against your own panel. The defaults above match a Cheap Yellow Display (ESP32-2432S028); a different board (or unit) may need different values.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Input — a raw RGB565-encoded buffer, exactly width * height * 2 bytes, the same format framebuf.FrameBuffer produces for an RGB565 surface. A wrong-length buffer raises a clear error rather than silently desyncing the panel.

A message with a y key is a strip instead: whole rows, written starting at row y. The gui screen node sends strips, so a large display never needs a full frame in memory.

docs.title: RGB565 byte order
docs.text:
framebuf.RGB565 stores each pixel in CPU-native (little-endian on ESP32) byte order, but SPI TFT controllers including the ST7789 expect big-endian pixel bytes on the wire. This node forwards whatever bytes it's given as-is, so a buffer built straight from framebuf.FrameBuffer(..., framebuf.RGB565) comes out with red and blue scrambled (an intended pure green circle renders red). There's no MicroPython-level flag to pick big-endian storage. Fix: byte-swap the buffer before handing it to this node —

for i in range(0, len(buf), 2):
    buf[i], buf[i + 1] = buf[i + 1], buf[i]

— right after drawing, before msg['payload'] = buf. A color whose two bytes match (pure white 0xFFFF, pure black 0x0000) is unaffected either way, which is why a swap bug can hide behind text and background colors.

docs.title: Indexed modes
docs.text:
Build an indexed frame with framebuf.FrameBuffer(..., framebuf.<FORMAT>), where <FORMAT> matches the frame format property:

frame format framebuf constant bits/pixel palette indices used 240×320 frame size rgb565 (default) RGB565 16 — (real color) 153,600 bytes gs4 GS4_HMSB 4 0–15 (all 16) 38,400 bytes gs2 GS2_HMSB 2 0–3 (first 4) 19,200 bytes mono MONO_HMSB 1 0–1 (first 2) 9,600 bytes

Send the bytearray itself as the payload (msg['payload'] = buf). bytes(buf) makes a second full-size copy the board may not have memory for. For a flow that redraws often, keep the buffer in context and reuse it.

Pixel values are palette indices, not colors — this node expands each one to real color using the palette property. Indexed modes have no byte-order gotcha: the palette already stores colors in the order this node expects.

The buffer isn't "1/N the size of RGB565": each row is padded to a whole number of bytes, so a width that isn't an exact multiple of the format's pixels-per-byte (2 for gs4, 4 for gs2, 8 for mono) needs slightly more than a flat width * height / bitsPerByte formula gives. This node works out and checks the real size, and names the expected byte count on a mismatch.

mono needs framebuf.MONO_HMSB specifically, not MONO_VLSB or MONO_HLSB. MicroPython's three 1-bit formats are not interchangeable — the wrong one silently produces a garbled image, not an error, because this node can't tell which you used. MONO_VLSB packs pixels into vertical byte columns (the OLED convention display i2c uses); this node streams rows, so MONO_VLSB won't work. MONO_HLSB and MONO_HMSB pack their 8 pixels-per-byte in opposite orders; this node expects MONO_HMSB, and MONO_HLSB comes out with each row's pixels in the wrong order.

Fewer colors as the depth drops, so these suit a UI with a fixed palette (buttons, status text, icons), not photos.

docs.title: ebutton
docs.text: Reports press, release, long-press, and double-click events from a single debounced button.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• pin — GPIO pin number. Default 5. Checked against your board.
  • pull — none (default), up, or down. Enables the board's own internal pull resistor on this pin.
  • sense — which electrical level means "pressed": auto (default, reads the pin's own boot state as "not pressed"), 0, or 1.
  • suppress — off by default. When on, press/release are held back until it's clear the click isn't the first half of a double — a plain single click still reports press then release, delayed by up to the double-click window; an actual double-click reports only double, not press/release for the first click too.
  • debounce (ms) — default 50ms.
  • long press (ms) — how long a press must hold to count as long. Default 1000ms.
  • double click (ms) — the window a second press must land in to count as double. Default 400ms. Must be less than long press.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
Each event sends one message, a dict with two keys:

msg = {'payload': 'press', 'topic': ''}
  • payload — the event that fired: press, release, long or double.
  • topic — empty.

With suppress off (the default), a press always reports immediately, whether or not a second press follows — so a rapid double-click reports both a press and a double, not double alone. Turn suppress on if a plain single press should never be reported when it turns out to be part of a double-click.

No internal pull is enabled by default — wire an external pull resistor, use a button module with one built in, or set pull if the button instead relies on the board's own internal pull-up/pull-down (a common case for boards with buttons wired straight to a GPIO with no resistor of their own — e.g. most of an EMF 2022 TiDAL badge's buttons).

Two ebutton nodes on the same pin share one button, so they must have the same settings, or the compile stops. See Hardware is shared.

docs.title: encoder
docs.text: Reads a quadrature encoder (a rotary knob) and sends its value each time it turns. Pin numbers are checked against your board.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• pin x / pin y — the encoder's two switch pins, read with internal pull-ups.
  • divide by (div) — the pulses in one detent: 4 or 2 for a mechanical knob's clicks, 1 for every pulse.
  • start value — the value it starts from.
  • lowest / highest — optional limits; the value stops at them (blank for none).
  • wrap at (mod) — optional: the value counts 0 to mod - 1 and wraps (blank for none).
  • settle (ms) — how long to wait for motion to stop; also the shortest gap between messages.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Output — the value, with the change since the last message:

msg = {'payload': 0, 'topic': '', 'delta': 0}

payload is the current value; delta is how far it moved, positive or negative.

Two encoder nodes on the same pins share one encoder, so they must have the same settings, or the compile stops. See Hardware is shared.

docs.title: eswitch
docs.text: Reports when a debounced switch opens or closes. Polling-based, not the interrupt-driven interrupt node.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• pin — GPIO pin number. Default 4. Checked against your board.
  • pull — none (default), up, or down. Enables the board's own internal pull resistor on this pin.
  • open level (lopen) — which electrical level means "open": 1 (default, switch to ground, pulled up) or 0 (switch to 3V3, pulled down).
  • debounce (ms) — how long a level must hold before it's accepted as real. Default 50ms.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
Each transition sends one message, a dict with two keys:

msg = {'payload': True, 'topic': ''}
  • payload — the switch state: true when closed, false when open.
  • topic — empty.

payload is a bool, so it wires straight to gpio out to mirror the switch.

No internal pull is enabled by default — wire an external pull resistor, use a switch module with one built in, or set pull if the switch instead relies on the board's own internal pull-up/pull-down.

Two eswitch nodes on the same pin share one switch, so they must have the same settings, or the compile stops. See Hardware is shared.

docs.title: filter
docs.text: Passes a message on only when it's worth sending, and drops the rest. Messages that pass are unchanged.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• mode — what counts as worth sending:
    • change — the payload differs from the last one passed.
    • deadband — the payload is a number that has moved at least threshold from the last one passed, up or down.
    • rate — at least interval has passed since the last message passed.
  • threshold — for deadband. A number of 0 or more. 0 passes any change.
  • interval (ms) — for rate.
  • ignore first message — for change and deadband. The first message only sets the starting value.
  • separately for each topic — on by default. Each msg.topic is filtered on its own.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
Deadband compares with the last value it let through, not the last one it received. A slow drift is passed once it adds up to the threshold.

Deadband reads text such as "21.5" as a number, so it works on MQTT payloads. The message still goes out as the original text. Anything else, including true/false, is dropped. The first time that happens, the node reports an error; the flow keeps running.

rate drops extra messages. It doesn't queue them or send them later.

A node tracks up to 32 topics. After that it forgets them all and starts again, and says so once in the console.

Everything resets when you deploy or the board restarts.

A temperature sensor read every second, into filter in deadband mode with threshold 0.5, into mqtt publish, tells the broker only about changes of half a degree or more.

docs.title: function
docs.text: Runs your own MicroPython on each message. Use it for anything a dedicated node type doesn't cover.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• code — the function body, run once per incoming message. msg is a dict; msg['payload'] is what you'll usually read and write. Return the (possibly modified) message to pass it on, or nothing to stop it there.
  • outputs — how many outputs the node has (outputCount in the flow file, up to 10).

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
One input, any message. With more than one output, return an array to route to specific outputs, Node-RED style:

if msg['payload'] > 100:
    return [msg, None]   # output 1 only
else:
    return [None, msg]   # output 2 only
  • None in a slot sends nothing out that output.
  • A plain return msg (no array) always targets output 1.
  • A slot holding a list of messages sends all of them out that one output, in order: return [[msg1, msg2], None].
  • Returning fewer elements than the node has outputs leaves the missing ones as None; returning more ignores the extras.

docs.title: Context, flow and settings
docs.text:
Three ways to keep state across messages, all available as plain objects inside your code:

  • context — private to this one function node. Use it for a counter or running total only this node needs.
  • flow — shared across the whole flow. flow.set('name', value) / flow.get('name') works from any function node, and reads/writes the same store a change node uses by name.
  • settings — saved on the board and survives a reboot. Use it for a value the user changes, such as units or a colour scheme. It is namespaced by the flow's name, so a different flow cannot read or overwrite it. settings.get('units', 'kg') / settings.set('units', 'lbs').
count = context.get('count', 0) + 1
context.set('count', count)
msg['payload'] = count
return msg

docs.title: gpio out
docs.text: Drives a GPIO pin high or low based on an incoming message.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text: • pin — GPIO pin number. Checked against your board.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text: A truthy payload sets the pin high, a falsy one sets it low, using Python's own truth test. 0, "", None and False are low; a bool input works as you'd expect, and other types convert to one of the two.

docs.title: GUI nodes
docs.text: Show readings on a display as pages of labels, numbers, bars and lights. Lay out the pages in the gui screen node's property panel: see Laying out pages.

docs.title: The nodes
docs.text:
• gui screen — one per display. Sends the screen each time it changes, in strips of about 5 KB, so a whole frame never has to fit in memory at once. Wire it to a display spi node: the screen takes its width, height and frame format from that display, so set them once on the display. To use touch, pick a touch panel in its properties.
  • gui readout — shows msg.payload as a number with units. Set the lowest and highest value it will show, and how many decimals. Its space is sized for that range. An optional caption puts a small muted line above the number ("Temperature"), which is the card-friendly way to label it.
  • gui label — shows msg.payload as text.
  • gui bar — a bar that fills between empty at and full at. Its style is solid (the outline) or segments: a row of cells, lit in the accent colour and unlit in the track, with a cell count to set.
  • gui trend — a moving histogram: a row of bars, oldest on the left, newest on the right. See Trend.
  • gui light — on when msg.payload is true, off when false. Its style is light (the circle) or chip: a filled pill showing a short word, with the on and off text both editable ("OK"/"Off").
  • gui button — a touch button. It has an input, which sets what it shows, and an output, which sends when it is tapped. See Buttons.
  • gui navigator — changes the page from the flow. Send next, prev, back, home or a page name. Sends the new page name when it changes. It isn't in the palette; a navigate button does the same from the screen.
  • gui modal — a full-screen message. Send any payload to open it, None to close it. If several are open, the highest priority shows and the rest wait. Its output sends how it closed: {topic: <modal's name>, payload: 'ack' | 'timeout' | 'closed'}. Properties: screen (the id of the gui_screen it belongs to), priority, and timeout in seconds (0 never closes by itself). The modal's layout is under its screen in the flow file, see Modals in the flow file.

Each widget starts as -- until a value arrives. With stale after set, a value that isn't updated in time is dimmed (or underlined, on a black-and-white display), so an old reading never looks current.

On a classic ESP32 without PSRAM, a GUI flow needs the custom firmware for classic ESP32: stock MicroPython runs out of memory loading the display stack.

docs.title: Trend
docs.text:
Shows what a number can't: which way it is heading. Wire it to the first output of a journal, or to any node that sends a list of numbers (a None is a gap), such as a spectrum from a function node.

Each bar is a row's average, in the theme's accent colour, with a thin line from the row's min to its max in the muted colour — so the range reads as context behind the value. A gap is empty. A wider space shows more history: it draws as many bars as fit, newest at the right edge.

  • bottom at / top at — the range of the bars. Values outside are cut off at the edge. The range is fixed.
  • columns, column width, height — the natural size: it is as wide as columns times column width, plus the border. In a layout it can stretch, and then shows more rows.
  • stale after — dims the bars if nothing new arrives in this time.

docs.title: Buttons
docs.text:
A button's mode says what a tap does.

  • momentary — sends its value: {topic: <the button's topic>, payload: <its sends value>}. The board label is only the text drawn on the button (blank: the flow label); sends is what leaves the output.
  • toggle — sends the opposite of its state. It shows its on and off text.
  • navigate — changes page: next, prev, back, home or a page name. It needs no wires.

Its style draws it as box (the outline, unchanged), filled (a solid accent button for the main action), or switch (a toggle drawn as a track and knob — it needs the toggle mode).

A button sends when your finger lifts inside it. Lift outside and nothing is sent. Set send on to press to send as soon as it is touched. It is drawn inverted while held.

Leave the value fields blank and a button sends true and false; for text, ON and OFF; for a number, 1 and 0. The gray placeholder shows which. Type a value to send something else.

A button needs a touch panel on its screen to be pressed. Deploy warns if a screen has buttons and no panel, and if a momentary or toggle button's output goes nowhere.

docs.title: A toggle that follows the real device
docs.text:
Wire the toggle's input to the device's real state, and its output to whatever switches it:

mqtt subscribe (stat/plug/POWER) -> toggle -> mqtt publish (cmnd/plug/POWER)

With the input wired, the flow owns the state:

  • Before the first report the toggle shows -- (a dashed outline).
  • A tap shows the state you asked for, with a dotted outline, until the input confirms it.
  • If the input says something different, the toggle shows what the input says.
  • If nothing comes back in time, it returns to the last known state, shows a cross for a moment, and the console reports it. See a toggle goes back.

The input is matched against the toggle's on sends and off sends values. MQTT delivers text, so the text true matches a true/false toggle and 1 matches a number toggle. Anything else shows --. Tasmota reports ON and OFF as text, so for a Tasmota plug set the value type to text and use ON and OFF.

Unwired, the toggle keeps its own state and starts as set by starts on.

docs.title: Color
docs.text: Set the display's frame format to rgb565 for full color. White text, gray for stale values, and a green accent for bars and lights that are on. Grays use less memory and send faster, so use them on boards with little RAM.

docs.title: Seven-segment digits
docs.text: The seg7 fonts (font_seg748, font_seg764, font_seg796) have only 0-9 : . - and a space, so they suit the time and time_seconds formats of the ntp node. On a 320-pixel-wide screen font_seg764 fits 14:05 (221 px) and font_seg748 fits 14:05:09 (254 px). font_seg796 is for wider screens. The font is DSEG by Keshikan (SIL Open Font License 1.1); see third-party licenses.

docs.title: Themes
docs.text:
By default a screen draws in the GUI's own colours. To choose your own, select the gui screen and set theme (a starting point) and any of the role colours in its Properties: the screen owns its look, and a screen with no theme keeps the default colours. An older flow may still use a shared GUI theme config; the screen's own colours win when both are set.

A theme is ten roles, so the widgets stay consistent and one theme works on different panels: background, card, foreground, muted (stale values), track (a bar's empty part), accent (bar fill, lights on), text on accent, ok, warn and alarm. Start from dark slate, light paper or vivid and change any colour; the preset is a starting point, not a lock. Vivid is the card demo's scheme: a near-black background, violet cards and a cyan accent.

Use the preset control in the theme's edit form to save your colours by name under ~/.thingstudio/presets/gui_theme/, and apply them to another theme later (Presets). The three starting points are built in, so a flow that names one still compiles without a backend.

A panel with fewer colours than that folds the roles onto the ones it has, rather than refusing the theme:

  • a gs4 panel (16 colours) gets every role as its own colour;
  • a gs2 panel (4 colours) keeps background, foreground, muted and accent — cards fold to the background, the track to muted, ok/warn/alarm to the foreground;
  • a mono panel (2 colours) is ink and paper: text, bars and lights are ink, backgrounds are paper.

A card is a panel behind a group of widgets: tick card on a row or column in the layout outline and its contents sit on a filled, rounded rectangle in the theme's card colour. It's the cheapest way to make a page read as groups rather than one list, and it follows the theme.

On an indexed panel (gs4, gs2 or mono) the theme also sets the display's palette while a screen is wired to it — one theme is the whole colour scheme, not two lists to keep in step. A palette set on the display itself is ignored while a themed screen is wired to it, and Deploy says so in the console.

docs.title: Rotating the screen
docs.text:
On the display node, set orientation to 0, 90, 180 or 270 (the picture turned clockwise). It is one setting on each display, so a display can't have two. Set the display's width and height to the panel's own size, and its rotation to how the panel is mounted (0 to 3). The gui screen wired to that display takes the display's size and turns its layout to match, and its touch axes follow. An orientation can't be combined with a panel offset (xstart/ystart, or the 135x240 panel). xstart/ystart of -1 mean "no offset" and are the right values with an orientation. At 90 or 270 the usable picture is the panel turned: 480 wide by 320 high on a 320x480 panel.

A flow that reads touch with a touch node instead of a gui screen sets the same angle on the node, since there is no display for it to follow.

docs.title: Modals in the flow file
docs.text:
A modal is laid out like a page, but in the screen's modals list, next to pages. Each entry names the gui_modal node and gives its layout as root. The modal node is not itself placed inside root; root holds only what the modal shows (text, and widget nodes wired to it or to the flow):

"screens": { "<screenId>": {
  "pages": [ ... ],
  "modals": [
    { "node": "<modalNodeId>", "root": { "kind": "column", "gap": 8, "padding": 8, "children": [
      { "kind": "text", "text": "Too hot", "font": "font_body24" },
      { "kind": "widget", "node": "<labelId>", "font": "font_body20", "maxChars": 20 }
    ] } }
  ]
} }

Send any payload to the modal node to open it; what is drawn is its layout, so wire a label or readout widget in the layout to the data you want shown (a modal can hold the same widget a page does). Send None to close it (a function node returning a message whose payload is None). A navigate button in the layout with target back acknowledges it, and a timeout above 0 closes it on its own. The modal node's output says which of the three happened.

docs.title: Laying out pages
docs.text:
Select the gui screen node and open Properties: each page is listed as an outline of its rows and columns, top to bottom in the order things appear on screen. Use ↑ and ↓ to move an element earlier or later, ⇥ to move it into the row or column above it, ⇤ to move it out of its container, ✕ to remove it, and ⚙ to set its font, grow, fill, gap, padding or card. Each row and column has a + add… menu: pick a widget, spacer, text, row, column or page dots and it goes at the end of that row or column. Add and reorder pages (the order of the page dots) from the page's own ↑ ↓, and add a layout for a modal. The same widget can be on several pages of a screen (a navigation button on every page, say). It must be drawn the same way on each, with the same font and options, and it shows the same value everywhere. Each page's + add… menu lists the widgets not already on that page. A widget belongs to one screen. Widgets in a row share it equally, so two buttons side by side are each half the row (never narrower than their text needs). Set grow to 0 on one to keep it at its natural size, or to a bigger number for a bigger share. The editor doesn't draw the page: if it doesn't fit, Deploy says which widget, on which page. The outline is a view of the flow file's "screens" section, which you can also edit by hand.

Tick fill on a row or column to give it the space left on the page (it sets grow: 1). Anything after a filling container keeps its natural height, so a plain row at the end of a page stays at the bottom: that is how a footer is made, and the page dots are just a widget you put in it. There is no separate footer setting, and a filling card stops above the row below it. The current page's dot is drawn as a pill, so it reads at a glance.

Pages live in the flow file, under "screens", keyed by the gui screen node's id. A page is a tree of row and column containers holding widgets ("kind": "widget", "node": "<id>"), fixed text, pagedots and spacers.

If something doesn't fit, Deploy stops and says which widget, on which page, needs how many pixels.

docs.title: http in
docs.text: Starts (or joins) an HTTP server on the device and fires a message for each matching incoming request.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• port — the TCP port to listen on (1–65535).
  • path — the exact path to match, e.g. /status. No named parameters: path matches one exact string (no /user/:id).
  • method — GET or POST. No other methods are supported.
  • response timeout (ms) — how long to wait for a paired http response node to actually reply before the request times out with a 500. Default 10000ms.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
Any number of http in nodes can share one port — each one claims its own exact (method, path) pair, and the device runs one shared server per port, routing each incoming request to whichever http in node matches. Two http in nodes claiming the same (method, path) on the same port is a compile error.

Fires once per matching request. The message carries req.method and req.path; payload is always None — the request body isn't parsed (see "Limitations" below). Pair every http in with a downstream http response node to actually answer the request — a request whose flow never reaches one gets a 500 automatically once the response timeout above elapses, rather than hanging the client forever.

A second request to the same route while an earlier one is still being processed queues behind it (this node processes one request at a time). Requests to different routes — even on the same port — are handled concurrently.

Uses the flow's WiFi network (its WiFi field, shared by every WiFi node).

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• No named path parameters. path matches one exact string, not Node-RED's /user/:name style.
  • No request body parsing. payload is always None; a POST/PUT body is read off the wire so it doesn't corrupt the next request, then discarded.
  • No cap on requests in flight. The device's own memory and socket limits apply, so this suits a handful of well-behaved clients rather than untrusted traffic.

docs.title: http request
docs.text: Makes one HTTP request per incoming message and returns the response.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• url — http://host[:port]/path. HTTPS isn't supported.
  • method — GET or POST. No other methods are supported.
  • timeout (ms) — how long to wait for the whole request/response exchange. Default 5000ms.
  • WiFi — the flow's WiFi network. Every WiFi node in a flow shares this one setting.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
For a POST, the incoming message's payload becomes the request body (a string is UTF-8 encoded; other types are converted). The first request goes out when the first message arrives, so a timer's first tick (one full interval after start) is the first request. The response comes back as the message's payload (the decoded body, as a string) and a status field (the HTTP status code).

When it goes wrong. A response with any status (404, 500, ...) is still sent on, with status set to that number (an integer), so test msg['status'] == 200 yourself. If the connection fails, the request times out or the reply can't be read, nothing is sent on: the node raises an error that shows in the debug log, and the next message tries again. To act on a failure, add a timer-driven check or watch the log; there is no failure output.

A few real limitations worth knowing: no HTTPS/TLS, no chunked transfer-encoding (the server needs to send Content-Length), no redirect following, and the response body must be valid UTF-8 — anything else raises rather than silently mangling it. The whole body is read into memory at once, so a response larger than the board's largest free block fails with MemoryError; request a smaller response or use a board with PSRAM. Uses the flow's WiFi network (its WiFi field, shared by every WiFi node).

docs.title: http response
docs.text: Completes a request that arrived via a matching http in node.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
None — everything comes off the message at runtime, same field names Node-RED uses:

  • msg.statusCode — the HTTP status code to send. Defaults to 200 if not set.
  • msg.payload — the response body. A string is UTF-8 encoded; other types are converted; None sends an empty body.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
Must fire on a message that originated from an http in node — firing it on any other message (one built from scratch, or one whose originating request already got its response) raises a clear error rather than failing silently.

The response is sent as plain bytes/text with no Content-Type header. Add one on the client side if you need to interpret the body as JSON.

docs.title: I2C bus
docs.text:
An I2C bus is shared by one or more devices. A display and a sensor can sit on the same bus, each at its own address.

Each I2C node has an I2C bus field. Pick a bus, or add one with +. The pins and clock are set once, on the bus, and every node on that bus uses them.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
• bus — the chip's I2C peripheral number, usually 0. Each bus number can be used once per flow.
  • scl pin / sda pin — the GPIO pins. Checked against your board.
  • frequency (Hz) — the clock. 100000 suits most sensors. Displays often run at 400000.

Changing a bus changes it for every node on it. If two buses end up with the same number, Deploy says so.

docs.title: In a function node
docs.text: runtime.shared('i2c', 0) returns the flow's bus 0, already set up. Use it to talk to a device that has no node of its own. It fails if no node in the flow uses that bus.

docs.title: i2c device
docs.text: Talks to an I2C device that has no node of its own. Each message that arrives does one transfer.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• I2C bus — the bus the device is wired to. See I2C bus.
  • operation — read, write or scan.
  • address — the device's address, such as 0x29. Not used by scan.
  • register — the register to read or write, such as 0x80. Leave empty for a device without registers.
  • length — for read, how many bytes.

Hex (0x29) and decimal (41) both work.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Input — for write, the bytes to send in payload. read and scan need no input.

Output — depends on the operation:

  • read — payload is the bytes read. Reading register 0x92 at address 0x29 (a TCS34725 ID register) returns b'D'.
  • write — sends payload and passes the message on unchanged. The payload can be bytes, a list of numbers 0–255, or one number.
  • scan — payload is the list of addresses that answer.

Other message fields are kept.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text: If a transfer fails, the node sends nothing and its status dot says why. The next message tries again.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
• disconnected — nothing answers at that address.
  • error — the payload can't be written.

docs.title: inject
docs.text: Fires once, with a fixed payload, when you click its "▶" icon while connected to a board. Click anywhere else on the node to open its property panel instead.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• payload type — bool, number, or string.
  • value — the fixed value to send, matching the chosen type.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text: The "▶" icon and the rest of the node are two separate click targets. The icon fires — only while live-connected, and only that one message; there's no periodic firing and no automatic fire-at-boot. The node body opens the property panel, live or not, so you can edit a flow's inject values without disconnecting first.
