A freshly deployed flow with only inject sources does nothing until you click one. To send a message automatically when the flow starts, use startup.

docs.title: interrupt
docs.text: Fires immediately when a GPIO pin changes state — genuinely event-driven, not polled.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• pin — GPIO pin number. Checked against your board.
  • edge — rising, falling, or both.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
The payload is the pin's level (true/false) at the moment the node wakes — a level, not a record of every intermediate change.

No internal pull resistor is configured. Wire an external pull resistor, or use a button module with one built in.

For a debounced switch or button, use eswitch or ebutton — they ignore contact bounce. interrupt is the raw edge node.

Two interrupt nodes on the same pin must have the same edge, or the compile stops. See Hardware is shared.

docs.title: journal
docs.text: Keeps the recent history of a number, as rows of average, minimum and maximum, the way RRDtool and Cacti do. Wire it to a trend to see the history, and to another journal for a longer time scale.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• rows kept — how many rows the history holds, 1 to 256. At 12 bytes a row, 156 rows is under 2 KB.
  • seconds per row — a row is closed once this much time has passed, and holds the average, min and max of the readings in it. 0 makes every message one row, which is what a journal fed by another journal wants.
  • rows per roll-up — 0 sends no roll-up.
  • gaps allowed in a roll-up — from 0 to 1, default 0.5. If more than this fraction of the rows in a roll-up are gaps, the roll-up is a gap too (payload of None). Averages use the known rows only; a gap is never counted as zero.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
• Input — msg.payload is a number. None records a gap. A message that carries min and max (the roll-up of another journal) is folded in with them, so a longer time scale keeps the spikes.
  • Output 1, series — sent each time a row is added. The payload is the journal itself, to wire to a trend. It is the live history, not a copy, so it costs no memory per row.
  • Output 2, roll-up — sent every rows per roll-up rows: payload the average, min, max, and the input's topic. Wire it to another journal, a readout or MQTT.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
A gap is empty, never a copy of the last value. The history starts empty each time the flow starts.

With seconds per row set, a row closes when a message arrives after its time is up, so a sensor that has gone quiet adds no gaps until it speaks again. Set the trend's stale after to dim it meanwhile. Choose a row longer than your sensor's interval (10 seconds for a reading every 5): a row that happens to catch no reading is a gap.

A payload that isn't a number is dropped. The first time that happens, the node reports an error; the flow keeps running.

docs.title: Cascading two journals
docs.text:
A sensor reads every 5 seconds.

  1. Journal A: rows 156, seconds per row 10, rows per roll-up 6. Its first output goes to a trend: the last 26 minutes.
  2. Journal B, fed from A's second output: rows 156, seconds per row 0. Its first output goes to a second trend: the last 2.6 hours, one bar a minute, each with its min to max line.

test-flows/gui-headliner-sensor-freenove-s3-4in.flow.json does this with a BME280.

docs.title: mqtt publish
docs.text: Publishes a message's payload to an MQTT topic.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• topic — the topic to publish to. Required.
  • retain — publish as a retained message.
  • QoS — 0 or 1. QoS 2 isn't supported.
  • broker — which MQTT broker config to use (see Editor in depth). Required — won't compile without one.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
Uses the flow's WiFi network (the WiFi config in the flow, shared by every WiFi node; the node's WiFi field selects that same network) and its own broker config for the MQTT connection. Nodes on the same broker share one connection. In a flow with MQTT nodes, MQTT manages the WiFi connection. An "unmanaged" WiFi config isn't accepted here: this node manages its own WiFi reconnection, so it needs a real network to connect to. The payload is sent as bytes (a string is UTF-8 encoded, other types are converted).

Shows a connection-status dot on the canvas (see Editor in depth) once connected to a device. It reports its own broker connection state, even when it shares that broker with an mqtt subscribe node. The node opens its broker connection only when there's actually something to publish, so the dot stays blank until the first message reaches it, even if the flow has been running a while.

docs.title: mqtt subscribe
docs.text: Emits one message per incoming message on a subscribed MQTT topic. With dynamic subscription on, its input changes the subscriptions while the flow runs.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• topic — the topic to subscribe to. Required.
  • QoS — 0 or 1. QoS 2 isn't supported.
  • dynamic subscription — accept subscribe/unsubscribe messages on the input (see below). Off by default.
  • broker — which MQTT broker config to use (see Editor in depth). Required — won't compile without one.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
The node subscribes to topic when the flow starts, and keeps it subscribed.

Uses the flow's WiFi network and its own broker config, same as mqtt publish. An "unmanaged" WiFi config isn't accepted here, for the same reason.

The message carries the payload (decoded as text when possible, raw bytes otherwise), the actual topic it arrived on, and whether the broker sent it as a retained message.

Dynamic subscription. With it on, an input message changes what the node listens to:

  • msg.action is subscribe or unsubscribe.
  • msg.topic is a topic string, a {topic, qos} object, or a list of either.

unsubscribe stops the node receiving that topic. Two nodes subscribed to the same topic are independent: one unsubscribing doesn't stop the other. The configured topic is subscribed at start, so turning dynamic subscription on doesn't interrupt anything; an unsubscribe for it takes effect until the next reload.

With dynamic subscription off, a message on the input raises an error rather than being ignored. An unknown action, or an action without a topic, raises an error too.

A subscription isn't guaranteed to be fully confirmed before an mqtt publish node on the same broker sends its first message. This is usually not an issue, but an early publish can go unheard by a subscriber that was still connecting.

Shows a connection-status dot on the canvas (see Editor in depth) once connected to a device, same as mqtt publish.

docs.title: neopixel
docs.text: Drives a WS2812 / NeoPixel strip: sets the pixels from each message and writes. Uses MicroPython's built-in neopixel module. Pin numbers are checked against your board.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• pin — the strip's data pin.
  • count — how many pixels.
  • order — the wire colour order of your strip: GRB (most WS2812), RGB, RGBW or GRBW.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Input — a colour, or a set of them:

msg = {'payload': 0xff4400, 'topic': ''}                         # the whole strip
msg = {'payload': [0xff0000, 0x00ff00, 0x0000ff], 'topic': ''}   # one colour per pixel
msg = {'payload': {'index': 2, 'colour': 0x00ff00}, 'topic': ''} # one pixel

A colour is a 24-bit 0xRRGGBB (red, green, blue, 0–255 each). An RGBW or GRBW strip takes a 32-bit 0xWWRRGGBB for the white channel; a plain 0xRRGGBB leaves white off.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
The whole strip is written on every message, so the last message sets the colours. The node has no output.

Two neopixel nodes on the same pin share one strip, so they must have the same count and order, or the compile stops. See Hardware is shared.

docs.title: ntp
docs.text: Sets the board's clock from the internet and sends the time, as text for a display or as Unix time.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• NTP server — default pool.ntp.org.
  • UTC offset (hours) — for standard time in your zone, for example 1 for central Europe or 5.5 for India.
  • daylight saving — UK / EU: automatic adds an hour from 01:00 UTC on the last Sunday of March to 01:00 UTC on the last Sunday of October. none leaves the offset alone. For other countries' rules, set the offset yourself.
  • format — what goes in payload. Each message also carries every format as a field of the same name.
  • WiFi — the flow's WiFi network, shared by every WiFi node.
format payload time 14:05 time_seconds 14:05:09 time_12h 2:05 pm date Wed 14 Oct date_iso 2026-10-14 iso 2026-10-14T14:05:09+01:00 unix 1791983109, an int: seconds since 1970 UTC, whatever the offset

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
• Input — any message asks for the time now. Wire a timer in for a clock that ticks: 1 second with seconds shown, otherwise 1 to 5 seconds.
  • Output — one message after each sync, and one for each input once the board has the time. Nothing is sent before the first sync, so a label shows -- rather than a wrong time.

To show the time and the date on one screen, use two ntp nodes, one with format time and one with date.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
The ntp node joins the flow's WiFi itself. Once WiFi is up it asks the NTP server for the time, tries again every 30 seconds until it works, and then every hour. Between syncs the board's own clock keeps time. The request takes up to a second and holds up the flow while it runs.

The board's clock is kept in UTC. The offset and summer time are added to each message, so the hour changes on time.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: The node's status shows waiting for WiFi, synced, or NTP from server failed. The first failure in a row also goes to the console. A board whose MicroPython has no ntptime module says so instead of failing at start. A flow with no WiFi network doesn't compile.

docs.title: pwm out
docs.text: Drives a PWM signal on a GPIO pin — for dimming an LED, driving a motor, or anything else that wants a variable duty cycle rather than a plain on/off.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• pin — GPIO pin number. Checked against your board.
  • frequency (Hz) — the PWM frequency. Default 1000Hz.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text: The input is a duty fraction from 0.0 (always off) to 1.0 (always on). A value outside that range is clamped rather than rejected — a slightly-out-of-bounds computed value won't crash the flow.

docs.title: startup
docs.text: Sends one message with a fixed payload each time the flow starts.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• payload type — bool, number, string, or start reason.
  • value — the fixed value to send, matching the chosen type. Not used with start reason.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Output — the fixed value, with a reason field saying why the flow started. With payload type start reason, the payload is that same string.

reason the flow started because deploy you clicked Deploy power_on the board was powered up hard_reset the reset button was pressed watchdog a watchdog timer reset the board deep_sleep the board woke from deep sleep soft_reset software restarted the board, for example machine.reset() unknown the board can't tell

Not every board reports every reason. ESP32 boards report the reset button as power_on, because on those chips the button cuts power to the core.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
The flow starts after every Deploy, and again whenever the board resets or powers up with a saved flow. So startup runs even when the editor isn't connected. Use it for setup work, such as setting an output to a known state or drawing a first screen.

It fires once per start and never repeats. For a message you trigger by hand, use inject. For a repeating one, use timer.

docs.title: timer
docs.text: Emits an increasing count on a fixed interval — a heartbeat with a sequence number, not a repeated value.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text: • interval (ms) — how often to emit. Must be a positive number.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text: The payload is a whole number that starts at 1 and increases by one on every tick — not a fixed constant. Each timer node keeps its own independent counter, even if two of them share the same interval.

docs.title: touch
docs.text:
Raw touch input, for flows that don't use the GUI. It reads a capacitive touch panel and sends a message when a finger lands and when it lifts.

A gui screen reads its panel itself, so you don't need this node to press buttons. One panel can't be used by both a gui screen and a touch node: Deploy stops and names them.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• touch panel — which touch panel to read. Pick one, or add one with +.
  • orientation — the turn of the picture these touches match: 0, 90, 180 or 270 degrees clockwise, the same four angles a display's orientation takes. Set it when the screen is turned and the flow reads touch through this node. Off leaves the panel's own axes alone. A flow with a gui screen sets orientation on the display instead and leaves this off: the screen turns its own touches to match.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Output — down and up, each with the touch point:

msg = {'payload': {'x': 120, 'y': 340}, 'topic': 'down'}   # a finger lands
msg = {'payload': {'x': 121, 'y': 338}, 'topic': 'up'}     # it lifts, where it was last seen

Down and up only: nothing is sent while the finger moves, and only one finger is followed. The coordinates are screen pixels in the turned picture, so they match what the display shows when the orientation is set (and in the panel's own axes when it is off). There is nothing to calibrate.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text: The status dot shows whether the panel is answering (FT6336U, or no reply from FT6336U at 0x38 on I2C bus 0). A missing panel sends nothing and is picked up when it appears. A panel that disappears mid-touch still sends its up.

docs.title: Touch panels
docs.text:
A touch panel is a capacitive touch screen on an I2C bus. Its settings are set once, in a config node, and a gui screen or a touch node picks it.

On a gui screen, pick the panel in the screen's properties. The screen reads it itself and turns touches into button presses. There is no wire to draw. If the panel stops answering, the screen's status dot says so, and any button being held is let go without sending.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
• controller — the touch chip. Supported hardware lists the chips covered (the FT6336U, as on the Freenove ESP32-S3 displays).
  • I2C bus — the bus the panel is wired to. See I2C bus. On the Freenove 4.0" board: SDA 16, SCL 15.
  • address — the chip's I2C address. 0x38 for the FT6336U.
  • reset pin — the panel's reset pin, if it has one (Freenove: 18). Blank for none.
  • poll every (ms) — how often to look. 20 is smooth; more than 50 starts to feel slow.
  • panel width / height — the panel's own size in pixels (Freenove: 320 × 480).
  • swap x and y / flip x / flip y — turn the panel's coordinates into the display's. If the display is rotated, tick these until a touch lands where you pressed.

docs.title: Presets
docs.text: The touch panel's edit form has a preset control, like the display nodes. Fill in the settings once, press the disk button, and give the set a name (for example freenove-4in). In another flow, open a new touch panel and pick that name to fill the form. The I2C bus is not saved, since it belongs to the flow; pick or add it after loading.

docs.title: Rotated screens
docs.text: If the display the gui screen is wired to has an orientation, the screen's touch axes are turned to match the picture. The raw touch node is not turned.

docs.title: Other touch chips
docs.text: For a chip this node doesn't cover, such as GT911 or CST820, read it from a function node with runtime.shared('i2c', 0), using the chip's datasheet and a MicroPython driver for it. See docs.micropython.org for the I2C calls.

docs.title: udp receive
docs.text: Listens on a UDP port and emits one message per datagram received.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• port — local port to listen on (1–65535).
  • poll interval (ms) — internal receive polling cadence. Default 20ms; rarely needs changing.
  • WiFi — the flow's WiFi network. Every WiFi node in a flow shares this one setting.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text: Uses the flow's WiFi network (its WiFi field, shared by every WiFi node). The payload is the raw bytes received, unparsed — decode it yourself in a function node if you're expecting text or a structured format. host and port fields on the message carry the sender's address, alongside the payload.

docs.title: udp send
docs.text: Sends a message's payload as a UDP datagram to a fixed host and port.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• host — destination hostname or IP.
  • port — destination port (1–65535).
  • timeout (ms) — how long to wait before giving up on the send. Default 2000ms.
  • WiFi — the flow's WiFi network. Every WiFi node in a flow shares this one setting.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
Uses the flow's WiFi network (its WiFi field, shared by every WiFi node). The payload is sent as bytes (a string is UTF-8 encoded, other types are converted); nothing about its content is validated.

A send that fails — an unreachable host, a DNS failure, a timeout — raises a clear error naming the host and port it was trying to reach, not a bare error code.

docs.title: wifi gate
docs.text: Passes a message through unchanged if the WiFi station is currently connected, or drops it if it isn't.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text: • WiFi — the flow's WiFi network. Every WiFi node in a flow shares this one setting.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
A transform, like function or delay — one input, one output, same msg in and out unchanged when the WiFi link is up. When the link is down, the message is dropped: nothing propagates past this node, the same way a function node's return None stops a message.

Uses the flow's WiFi network (its WiFi field, shared by every WiFi node).

This checks the WiFi station's live link state at the moment each message arrives, not a value read off wifi status's own output messages. wifi status only emits when its connection identity changes, so a fast-firing source (a timer or sensor) gated off wifi status's wire could be checking stale state. This node reads the hardware directly, so it always answers "is the link up right now."

A GPIO, timer or sensor source fires on its own schedule with no awareness of whether WiFi is up. Put a wifi gate between that source and whatever sends the result over the network: messages that arrive while the link is down are dropped instead of failing downstream (or queuing for a retry a node like http request might otherwise attempt).

This only checks the WiFi link itself — not whether a specific MQTT broker or HTTP server is reachable beyond that. mqtt publish, mqtt subscribe and http request already handle their own connection lifecycle on top of a working WiFi link.

docs.title: wifi status
docs.text: Reports the board's WiFi connection state. In a flow with no other WiFi node, it also brings the connection up.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• poll interval (ms) — how often to check the connection. Default 5000ms.
  • WiFi — the flow's WiFi network. Every WiFi node in a flow shares this one setting (see Editor in depth).

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
This node is optional: other network nodes don't need it. In a flow with MQTT nodes, MQTT manages the WiFi connection and this node only reports on it.

The payload is true/false for connected/disconnected. The message also carries ip, subnet, gateway, dns (all empty strings when disconnected), and rssi (signal strength in dBm, or null when disconnected or when the board doesn't support reading it — RSSI is an ESP32-only reading, not available on every board). Use a debug node with "full message" checked to see all of these — by default debug only prints payload.

It emits when connection identity changes (connect/disconnect, or a change to ip/subnet/gateway/dns), not on every poll — except the very first poll, which always reports. rssi doesn't trigger a re-emit on its own — it drifts constantly even on an idle connection, so it's included whenever a message fires for another reason, but its own changes don't cause one. Pick "unmanaged" on the WiFi config when you don't want this node issuing its own connect — either because something else already manages the connection, or because you want the device to learn its credentials on its own over the air. See WiFi provisioning for how that self-provisioning flow works, including the setup network's password and the reprovisioning-fallback option.

If no connection is ever made, this node reports disconnected, the same as any other failed connect — provisioning changes how the interface gets its credentials, not how wifi_status reports on them.
